lectures.title: Visual function, visual pathway & colour vision
key: Visual acuity (VA) = central (macular, cone) vision; measured with an optotype at 5 m: VA = d/D (e.g. 5/50 = 0.1); normal = 1 (10/10, 20/20)
Low vision steps: reduce distance (4/50…1/50) → counting fingers → hand movements → light perception (with/without projection) → no light perception (NLP)
Pinhole: VA improves → refractive error; does not improve → organic disease (cataract, macula, optic nerve)
Rods: peripheral retina, night (scotopic) vision, rhodopsin; cones: macula/fovea, day (photopic) & colour vision, iodopsin
Visual pathway: optic nerve → chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → optic radiations → occipital cortex
Field defects: optic nerve = monocular (central scotoma); chiasm = BITEMPORAL hemianopia (pituitary adenoma); retrochiasmal = CONTRALATERAL HOMONYMOUS hemianopia
Visual field tests: confrontation, Amsler grid (central 10°, metamorphopsia), kinetic (Goldmann) & static automated perimetry (Humphrey)
Colour vision: congenital defects = X-linked (males), bilateral, symmetrical, stable, untreatable (protan = red, deutan = green, tritan = blue); acquired = asymmetric, progressive, may improve
Colour tests: Ishihara plates (red-green screening), Farnsworth D-15/100-hue (arrangement), anomaloscope (matching, diagnosis)
traps: Heteronymous (bitemporal) = chiasm; HOMONYMOUS = after the chiasm
A LEFT homonymous hemianopia = RIGHT hemisphere lesion
Congenital colour defects: more frequent in MALES, not unilateral, not treatable
Rods contain rhodopsin, cones iodopsin – not the opposite
gloss: area of lost vision inside the field
loss of half of the visual field

lectures.title: Refraction, accommodation & ametropias
key: Emmetropia: parallel rays focus ON the retina without accommodation
Myopia: focus IN FRONT of the retina (long axial length / strong power) → divergent (concave, minus) lenses; good near vision; risks: RD, myopic maculopathy, glaucoma, early cataract
Hyperopia: focus BEHIND the retina (short eye) → convergent (convex, plus) lenses; accommodative asthenopia, accommodative esotropia, early presbyopia, angle closure
Astigmatism: different power in the meridians (toric cornea) → cylindrical (toric) lenses or rigid contact lenses
Presbyopia: PHYSIOLOGICAL loss of accommodation (~40–45 y) → blurred near vision → plus lenses for near; earlier in hyperopes, later in myopes
Anisometropia: different refraction between the eyes → amblyopia in children, aniseikonia
Aphakia: no lens → very high hyperopia; correction: IOL (best), contact lens, thick glasses (+10 D)
Accommodation = contraction of the ciliary muscle → zonule relaxes → lens rounder; cycloplegia (atropine, cyclopentolate, tropicamide) for objective refraction in children
Refractive surgery: LASIK/PRK (cornea), phakic IOL, clear lens extraction
traps: Myopia: the axis is LONGER, not shorter
Presbyopia is NOT pathological
Convergent lenses: hyperopia, presbyopia, aphakia – NOT myopia
Pilocarpine stimulates accommodation (miotic) – not a cycloplegic
gloss: nearest point seen clearly with maximal accommodation
different image size between the eyes

lectures.title: Binocular vision, strabismus & amblyopia
key: Worth degrees of binocular vision: 1 simultaneous perception → 2 fusion → 3 stereopsis
Heterophoria = latent deviation controlled by fusion (asthenopia, headache); heterotropia = manifest strabismus
Concomitant (non-paralytic) strabismus: children, same angle in all gazes, no diplopia (suppression) → AMBLYOPIA
Paralytic strabismus: acquired, DIPLOPIA, false projection, limited movement and larger angle in the field of the paralysed muscle, head turn
III palsy: ptosis + eye down & out + mydriasis (pupil-involving = aneurysm until proven otherwise); IV: vertical diplopia, head tilt; VI: esotropia, no abduction (diabetes, raised ICP)
Accommodative esotropia: hyperopia → corrected by full plus (convergent) glasses
Tests: Hirschberg (corneal light reflex), cover / uncover / alternate cover test, ocular motility in 9 gaze positions
Amblyopia = reduced best-corrected VA without lesion: strabismic, anisometropic, deprivation (congenital cataract, ptosis); treatment before 7–8 y: correct refraction + OCCLUDE the good eye
Strabismus treatment order: glasses → amblyopia treatment → orthoptics → surgery (in childhood)
traps: Diplopia = PARALYTIC, not concomitant strabismus
Phoria: fusion PRESENT
Amblyopia must be treated BEFORE strabismus surgery
Esophoria (latent) does not give amblyopia
Diplopia worse to the right in a diabetic = RIGHT VI palsy
gloss: corneal light reflexes – estimate of the angle

lectures.title: Orbit: exophthalmos, cellulitis, thyroid eye disease, tumours
key: Exophthalmos (proptosis) = cardinal sign of orbital disease; measured with Hertel exophthalmometer (> 20 mm or > 2 mm asymmetry)
Most common cause of exophthalmos in adults (uni- or bilateral) = thyroid eye disease (Graves)
Preseptal cellulitis: lid oedema/erythema, NO proptosis, normal motility and VA

Orbital (post-septal) cellulitis: fever, PROPTOSIS, painful/limited eye movements, chemosis, ± decreased VA/RAPD; cause: ETHMOIDITIS (children) → IV antibiotics + CT; complications: abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, optic neuropathy

Thyroid eye disease: upper lid retraction (Dalrymple), lid lag (von Graefe), proptosis, restrictive myopathy (inferior & medial rectus) → diplopia, exposure keratopathy, compressive optic neuropathy; treatment: stop smoking, euthyroid, selenium, IV steroids / teprotumumab, radiotherapy, decompression
Orbital myositis (idiopathic inflammation): painful eye movements, diplopia → corticosteroids

Orbital tumours: slowly progressive non-axial/axial proptosis; children: capillary haemangioma, dermoid, rhabdomyosarcoma; adults: cavernous haemangioma, lymphoma, meningioma, metastases (breast → enophthalmos)
Enophthalmos: blow-out fracture of the orbital floor (infraorbital anaesthesia, limited upgaze), atrophy, scirrhous metastasis
traps: Proptosis distinguishes ORBITAL from PRESEPTAL cellulitis
Orbital cellulitis = inflammation of orbital FAT/soft tissue (not the periosteum)
Rhabdomyosarcoma: rapidly progressive proptosis in a child – urgent biopsy
gloss: orbital floor fracture with muscle entrapment

lectures.title: Lacrimal system: dry eye, dacryocystitis, dacryoadenitis
key: Tear film: lipid (meibomian glands), aqueous (lacrimal gland), mucin (goblet cells)

Dry eye: burning, foreign-body sensation, worse at the end of the day; Schirmer test (< 10 mm/5 min), tear break-up time (< 10 s), fluorescein/lissamine staining; Sjögren; treatment: artificial tears, lid hygiene, cyclosporine, punctal plugs
Epiphora = overflow of tears from impaired DRAINAGE (punctal ectropion, canalicular or nasolacrimal duct obstruction); lacrimation = hypersecretion
Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (valve of Hasner): epiphora + mucopurulent discharge from weeks of age; massage (Crigler) + antibiotic drops; persistent → PROBING (usually 12 months)
Acute dacryocystitis (adult): painful red swelling BELOW the medial canthal tendon, reflux of pus → systemic antibiotics, later dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR); risk of orbital cellulitis, fistula
Chronic dacryocystitis: epiphora + mucopurulent reflux on pressure; reservoir of bacteria (contraindicates intraocular surgery until treated)
Dacryoadenitis = inflammation of the lacrimal GLAND: upper-outer lid swelling, S-shaped ("horizontal S") lid; causes: mumps, EBV, bacterial, sarcoidosis
Tests of drainage: fluorescein dye disappearance, syringing/irrigation, Jones tests, dacryocystography
traps: DacryoCYSTitis = SAC (medial canthus); dacryoADENitis = GLAND (upper-outer)
Treatment of choice of congenital dacryocystitis = PROBING (not DCR)
Congenital glaucoma also gives tearing – check corneal size and photophobia
gloss: measures tear secretion with filter paper

lectures.title: Eyelids: blepharitis, chalazion, hordeolum, entropion, ectropion, ptosis, tumours
key: Blepharitis = chronic inflammation of the LID MARGINS: anterior (staphylococcal, seborrhoeic) / posterior (meibomian gland dysfunction); crusts, red margins, worse in the morning; treatment: warm compresses + lid hygiene, ± antibiotics, cautious steroids
Hordeolum (stye) = acute painful staphylococcal abscess: external (Zeis/Moll glands at lash follicle) or internal (meibomian gland); warm compresses ± antibiotic
Chalazion = chronic painless lipogranuloma of a meibomian gland; may resolve or need incision–curettage; recurrent at the same site → biopsy (sebaceous carcinoma)
Entropion: margin turned IN → trichiasis, corneal erosions/ulcer; involutional, cicatricial (trachoma, burns), spastic, congenital → surgery
Ectropion: margin turned OUT → epiphora, exposure keratitis; involutional (elderly), paralytic (VII palsy), cicatricial, mechanical → surgery
Lagophthalmos (incomplete closure): facial palsy, exophthalmos, ectropion → exposure keratitis → lubricants, taping, tarsorrhaphy
Ptosis: congenital (levator dystrophy → amblyopia risk), aponeurotic (elderly), neurogenic (III palsy, Horner), myogenic (myasthenia)
Eyelid tumours: basal cell carcinoma (most frequent, lower lid, medial canthus, pearly ulcerated nodule) > squamous, sebaceous carcinoma, melanoma; benign: xanthelasma, papilloma
traps: Chalazion is NOT an infection and is PAINLESS; hordeolum is acute and painful
VII palsy → paralytic ECTROPION (not entropion)
Spastic ectropion: acute conjunctival inflammation
gloss: sebaceous glands of the lash follicles

lectures.title: Conjunctiva: conjunctivitis, red eye, pterygium
key: Conjunctivitis: red eye with SUPERFICIAL (peripheral) congestion, discharge, foreign-body/sand sensation, itching; NORMAL VA, no pain, normal pupil & IOP
Viral (adenovirus, ~80 % of infections): watery discharge, follicles, tender pre-auricular node, URTI/fever, very contagious, self-limiting (antibiotics useless)
Bacterial: mucopurulent discharge, papillae, lids stuck in the morning → wash + antibiotic drops (chloramphenicol, tobramycin…)
Allergic: ITCHING, watery discharge, chemosis, papillae (giant papillae = cobblestones in vernal / contact-lens conjunctivitis) → antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops, cold compresses

Neonatal conjunctivitis: chemical (day 1), gonococcal (day 2–4, hyperpurulent, risk of perforation), chlamydial (day 5–14) → hospitalise + SYSTEMIC antibiotics; prophylaxis: erythromycin / povidone-iodine (historic AgNO3)
Adult inclusion conjunctivitis (Chlamydia D-K): chronic follicular → oral azithromycin/doxycycline (treat partner); trachoma (A-C) → scarring, entropion, trichiasis, blindness
Pseudomembranous: adenovirus, gonococcus, streptococcus; true membranes: diphtheria
NEVER patch an eye with conjunctivitis; DDx: keratitis, uveitis, acute glaucoma (deep ciliary injection + decreased VA)
Pterygium: fibrovascular wing-shaped growth from the nasal conjunctiva onto the cornea (UV) → surgery with conjunctival autograft; subconjunctival haemorrhage: harmless, check BP/coagulation
traps: Conjunctivitis does NOT reduce vision
Follicles + pre-auricular adenopathy = viral; giant papillae = allergic/contact lens
Neonatal conjunctivitis requires SYSTEMIC antibiotics
gloss: vascular core with inflammatory cells (bacterial, allergic)

lectures.title: Cornea & sclera: keratitis, ulcers, keratoconus, scleritis
key: Keratitis: painful red eye with CILIARY (perikeratic) injection, photophobia, tearing, DECREASED VA, fluorescein-positive lesion (epithelial forms), reflex miosis
HSV epithelial keratitis: DENDRITIC ulcer (fluorescein +), decreased corneal sensation, unilateral, recurrent → topical aciclovir/ganciclovir; STEROIDS CONTRAINDICATED
HSV stromal (disciform) keratitis: intact epithelium, stromal oedema → antivirals + topical steroids
Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1): elderly/immunocompromised, dermatomal rash; Hutchinson sign (nose tip) → ocular involvement → oral aciclovir high dose (800 mg ×5) / valaciclovir
Bacterial keratitis: contact lenses, trauma, ocular surface disease; white infiltrate, purulent discharge, hypopyon → scraping/culture, intensive fortified or fluoroquinolone drops
Fungal keratitis after plant trauma (feathery infiltrate); Acanthamoeba: contact lens + water, severe pain, ring infiltrate
Exposure (lagophthalmic) keratitis: VII palsy, exophthalmos, ectropion → inferior erosions; neurotrophic keratitis: V lesion → anaesthetic cornea
Keratoconus: progressive conical thinning, irregular astigmatism, young adults → glasses, rigid lenses, corneal cross-linking, keratoplasty
Episcleritis: benign, sectoral, mild discomfort; scleritis: deep violaceous, severe boring pain, associated with RA/vasculitis → systemic NSAIDs/steroids/immunosuppression
traps: Never steroids in EPITHELIAL herpetic keratitis
Dendritic = HSV; geographic = advanced HSV (often after steroids)
Stromal keratitis: fluorescein NEGATIVE
Decreased corneal sensitivity in HSV and neurotrophic keratitis
gloss: pus level in the anterior chamber

lectures.title: Uvea: anterior, intermediate & posterior uveitis, endophthalmitis
key: Anterior uveitis (iritis/iridocyclitis): pain, photophobia, decreased VA, CILIARY injection, MIOSIS, keratic precipitates, flare & cells, hypopyon, posterior synechiae (irregular pupil)
Cyclitis / intermediate uveitis: white or mildly red eye, floaters, vitreous/retrolental exudates ("snowballs"), fluctuating IOP

Posterior uveitis (choroiditis/retinochoroiditis): floaters, decreased VA, white eye; toxoplasmosis = white fluffy focus next to a pigmented scar ("headlight in the fog"); congenital form → macular scars
Causes: HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis), sarcoidosis, JIA (silent – screening), Behçet, infections (herpes, toxoplasma, TB, syphilis, Lyme), focal infections (dental/ENT)
Treatment: topical corticosteroids + MYDRIATICS/CYCLOPLEGICS (atropine, tropicamide – prevent synechiae, relieve pain) ± periocular/systemic steroids, immunosuppressants; NEVER miotics
Complications: posterior synechiae (seclusio pupillae → iris bombé → secondary glaucoma), complicated cataract, band keratopathy, cystoid macular oedema, hypotony, phthisis bulbi
Endophthalmitis: post-operative (cataract surgery), post-traumatic, endogenous (septicaemia), perforated ulcer → pain, hypopyon, vitritis → intravitreal antibiotics, vitrectomy
Sympathetic ophthalmia: bilateral granulomatous panuveitis after penetrating injury of one eye
traps: Uveitis is treated with MYDRIATICS, never miotics
Iritis: miosis + KP + hypopyon; cyclitis: white eye + vitreous exudates
Toxoplasmic retinochoroiditis: usually NO synechiae, white eye
gloss: keratic precipitates – inflammatory cells on the endothelium
adhesion of the iris (posterior: to the lens)

lectures.title: Lens: cataract, lens luxation, aphakia
key: Cataract = opacification of the lens: progressive painless blurred vision, glare, monocular diplopia, myopic shift (nuclear), abnormal red reflex / leukocoria

Types by cause: senile (most frequent: nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular), congenital (zonular/lamellar most common; rubella, galactosaemia), traumatic, complicated (uveitis, high myopia, RP, glaucoma, RD), metabolic (diabetes, hypocalcaemia, Wilson), drug-induced (STEROIDS)
Stages of senile cortical cataract: incipient → intumescent (phacomorphic angle-closure) → mature → hypermature (Morgagnian, phacolytic glaucoma, phaco-anaphylactic uveitis, lens luxation)
Treatment = surgery: phacoemulsification + foldable posterior chamber IOL; congenital dense cataract → early surgery (amblyopia)
Complications of surgery: endophthalmitis, posterior capsule rupture, cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment, posterior capsule opacification ("secondary cataract" → Nd:YAG capsulotomy)

Lens subluxation: iridodonesis/phacodonesis, unequal anterior chamber depth, vitreous in AC, monocular diplopia; luxation: lens in AC (acute glaucoma) or vitreous; causes: trauma, Marfan (up-temporal), homocystinuria (down), Weill-Marchesani
Aphakia: high hyperopia (+10 D) → IOL, contact lens or glasses
traps: Uncomplicated cataract never causes NLP – light perception with good projection persists
"Secondary cataract" = posterior capsule opacification after extracapsular surgery
Pinhole does NOT improve VA in dense/posterior subcapsular cataract

lectures.title: Intraocular pressure & aqueous humour
key: Aqueous produced by the ciliary processes (non-pigmented epithelium) → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → TRABECULAR meshwork → Schlemm canal (conventional, ~85 %) or uveoscleral outflow
Normal IOP 10–21 mmHg, daily variation < 5 mmHg (higher in the morning)
Tonometry: Goldmann applanation (gold standard, corrected for central corneal thickness), non-contact (air-puff), Schiøtz indentation, rebound (iCare), digital (palpation – rough estimate)
Gonioscopy: assesses the angle (open/closed, synechiae, neovessels)

Drugs lowering IOP: prostaglandin analogues (↑ uveoscleral outflow, 1×/day), β-blockers (↓ production), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (dorzolamide, acetazolamide), α2-agonists (brimonidine, contraindicated in infants), miotics (pilocarpine, ↑ trabecular outflow), osmotics (mannitol)
Hypotony (< 6 mmHg): wound leak, choroidal detachment, cyclitis, phthisis
traps: Tonometry is CONTRAINDICATED in an open globe
Thick cornea overestimates IOP, thin cornea underestimates it
Normal IOP does not exclude glaucoma (normal-tension glaucoma)
gloss: main outflow filter in the angle
circular canal draining aqueous to episcleral veins

lectures.title: Glaucoma: open-angle, angle-closure, congenital, secondary
key: Glaucoma = progressive optic neuropathy (cupping, rim loss) with characteristic VF defects; raised IOP is the main modifiable risk factor

POAG: bilateral, chronic, PAINLESS, asymptomatic until late; IOP 22–40, enlarged vertical cup (C/D > 0.5 or asymmetry), arcuate/Bjerrum & paracentral scotomas, nasal step → tunnel vision; VA preserved until late
POAG treatment: prostaglandin analogues first → combinations → SLT laser trabeculoplasty → trabeculectomy (when target IOP not reached or progression); lifelong follow-up (OCT, VF)

Acute angle closure (PACG): hyperopes, women, elderly, mydriasis/dim light; severe pain, headache, nausea/vomiting, haloes, red eye, corneal oedema, fixed mid-dilated VERTICAL OVAL pupil, shallow AC, IOP 50–80, rock-hard eye
Acute treatment: IV acetazolamide + mannitol, topical β-blocker, pilocarpine (after IOP drops), then LASER PERIPHERAL IRIDOTOMY in BOTH eyes (mandatory), ± lens extraction
Congenital glaucoma: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm, enlarged cloudy cornea (buphthalmos), Haab striae → SURGERY (goniotomy/trabeculotomy)
Secondary glaucomas: neovascular (PDR, ischaemic CRVO), phacomorphic/phacolytic, uveitic, steroid-induced, traumatic (hyphaema, angle recession), pigmentary, pseudoexfoliation
End-stage (absolute) glaucoma: blind (NLP), painful eye
traps: POAG is painless – pain points to angle closure
Angle closure: the pupil is MID-DILATED, not miotic
Iridotomy also in the FELLOW eye
Avoid mydriatics/anticholinergics in narrow angles
Neovascular glaucoma comes from retinal ISCHAEMIA (not keratitis, not cataract)
gloss: laser hole in the peripheral iris

lectures.title: Retina: vascular occlusions, diabetic retinopathy, AMD, detachment, tumours
key: CRAO: sudden painless near-total loss (counting fingers/LP), white oedematous retina, CHERRY-RED SPOT, thin arteries, RAPD; embolus/GCA → emergency (rule out giant cell arteritis: ESR/CRP)

CRVO: sudden painless decrease, "blood and thunder" fundus: flame haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots, disc & macular oedema; ischaemic form → neovascular glaucoma ("100-day"); treatment: anti-VEGF for macular oedema, PRP if neovessels

Diabetic retinopathy: NPDR (microaneurysms – first sign, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, IRMA, venous beading) → PDR (neovessels → vitreous haemorrhage, TRACTIONAL RD, neovascular glaucoma); maculopathy (oedema) = main cause of VA loss
DR treatment: glycaemia/BP/lipids control, anti-VEGF for macular oedema, panretinal photocoagulation for PDR, vitrectomy for haemorrhage/traction; screening yearly

AMD: > 50 y, smoking, genetics; CENTRAL vision (reading, faces), drusen early; dry/atrophic (geographic atrophy – AREDS vitamins, low-vision aids) vs wet/neovascular (sudden metamorphopsia → intravitreal anti-VEGF); Amsler grid self-monitoring

Rhegmatogenous RD: retinal BREAK + liquefied vitreous; risk: high myopia, lattice, PVD, cataract surgery, trauma; floaters + flashes + progressive curtain field defect; surgery (vitrectomy, scleral buckle, pneumatic retinopexy) – macula-on = emergency
Tractional RD: PDR, ROP, penetrating trauma; exudative RD: tumours, inflammation (Harada), toxaemia
Retinitis pigmentosa: night blindness, ring scotoma → tunnel vision, bone-spicule pigment, thin vessels, waxy pale disc, ERG extinguished
Retinoblastoma: RB1, children < 5 y, LEUKOCORIA (1st) then strabismus; choroidal melanoma: adults, brown elevated mass, exudative RD → brachytherapy / enucleation
Hypertensive retinopathy: arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, papilloedema (malignant)
traps: Cherry-red spot = CRAO (also Tay-Sachs); many haemorrhages = CRVO
PDR gives TRACTIONAL (not exudative or rhegmatogenous) detachment
AMD spares peripheral vision; anti-VEGF only for the WET form
Laser IRIDOTOMY is for angle closure; PANRETINAL photocoagulation is for PDR/ischaemic RVO

lectures.title: Optic nerve & pupil: neuritis, ischaemic neuropathy, papilloedema, atrophy
key: Optic neuritis (MS, young women): subacute VA loss, PAIN on eye movement, RAPD, red desaturation, CENTRAL/centro-caecal scotoma; retrobulbar form: normal disc ("the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing"); papillitis: swollen hyperaemic disc → MRI, IV methylprednisolone

AION non-arteritic: > 50 y, vascular risk factors, small crowded disc, sudden PAINLESS loss on waking, ALTITUDINAL (inferior) defect, swollen pale disc; arteritic (Giant cell/Horton): > 70 y, headache, jaw claudication, ESR/CRP ↑ → immediate high-dose steroids (risk to the other eye)
Papilloedema = bilateral disc swelling from raised ICP (tumour, IIH, hydrocephalus, venous thrombosis): VA preserved for long, transient obscurations, enlarged blind spot
Optic atrophy: pale disc, decreased VA/colour, RAPD; primary (compression, trauma), secondary/consecutive (after papilloedema, papillitis, retinal disease), glaucomatous (cupped)

Pupil: direct and consensual reflexes; afferent defect (RAPD, Marcus Gunn – swinging flashlight); AMAUROTIC rigidity (blind eye: no direct, consensual preserved); ABSOLUTE rigidity (efferent III lesion: no direct, no consensual)
Horner: miosis + ptosis + anhidrosis (sympathetic); Adie tonic pupil: dilated, slow; Argyll Robertson: small irregular, light-near dissociation (syphilis)
traps: Altitudinal defect = AION; central scotoma = optic neuritis; enlarged blind spot = papilloedema
Papilloedema term is reserved for raised ICP and keeps VA
Amaurotic rigidity: CONSENSUAL preserved
Optic atrophy without cupping ≠ glaucoma

lectures.title: Ocular trauma: burns, contusion, open globe, foreign bodies
key: CHEMICAL BURN = most urgent emergency: IMMEDIATE copious irrigation with water/saline (≥ 30 min, on the spot), check pH, remove particles; ALKALIS (liquefaction, deep) worse than ACIDS (coagulation)
Severity: limbal ischaemia (white eye = severe), corneal opacity; sequelae: symblepharon, vascularised leucoma, dry eye, glaucoma
Corneal abrasion / superficial foreign body: pain, photophobia, fluorescein +; vertical linear scratches = foreign body under the upper lid (evert the lid)

Blunt trauma (contusion): hyphaema, traumatic mydriasis, iridodialysis, angle recession, lens subluxation, commotio retinae (Berlin oedema), choroidal rupture, retinal tears/RD, vitreous haemorrhage, optic nerve avulsion, orbital blow-out fracture
Hyphaema: rest, head up, steroids, cycloplegics, IOP control; complications: rebleeding (day 3–5), glaucoma, corneal BLOOD STAINING
Open globe (penetrating/perforating): shield, NO pressure, no drops, tetanus + systemic antibiotics, CT, urgent primary watertight repair; risk: endophthalmitis, sympathetic ophthalmia
Intraocular foreign body: CT (not MRI if metallic); iron → siderosis, copper → chalcosis → always remove metallic IOFB
Physical burns: UV keratitis (welding, snow – punctate erosions hours later), thermal, radiation
traps: Irrigate FIRST – do not wait for the hospital or neutralise
Acid = coagulation; alkali = liquefaction
Never MRI with a suspected metallic IOFB
Most serious complication of hyphaema: corneal blood staining
gloss: fluorescein shows aqueous leak from a wound

lectures.title: Practical exam: history, examination techniques & the 15 lab subjects
key: History: chief complaint (decreased VA – sudden/progressive, red eye, pain, diplopia, floaters, flashes), onset, uni/bilateral, past ocular history, glasses, systemic diseases (diabetes, HT), drugs (steroids), family history (glaucoma)
VA: each eye separately, 5 m, uncorrected/corrected/pinhole; near VA; low vision steps
Confrontation field: examiner and patient 1 m apart, each eye, 4 quadrants – bitemporal vs homonymous hemianopia
Ocular motility: 9 gaze positions; cover test (tropia), uncover/alternate (phoria); Hirschberg
Anterior segment: flashlight + slit lamp – lids, conjunctiva (superficial vs ciliary injection), cornea (clarity, sensitivity with cotton wisp, fluorescein), AC depth, iris, pupil, lens
Pupil: size, shape, direct/consensual reflex, swinging flashlight (RAPD), near reflex
Red reflex (distant direct ophthalmoscopy): normal orange-red; dark opacities = media; white = leukocoria (retinoblastoma, cataract)
Digital tonometry: two index fingers through the closed upper lid – soft/normal/hard (rock-hard in acute glaucoma); contraindicated in open globe
Direct ophthalmoscopy: disc (colour, margins, C/D), vessels (A/V 2/3), macula; recognise DR, papilloedema, glaucomatous cupping, optic atrophy
traps: Measure VA BEFORE drops and light examination
Corneal sensitivity decreased in HSV and V palsy
Fluorescein stains EPITHELIAL defects (stromal keratitis negative)
gloss: retinal reflection seen through the pupil
parts: Lab – Examination of the anterior segment

sx: Bumping into objects on one side, difficulty reading (homonymous), often unnoticed bitemporal loss
ex: Confrontation test (each eye, 4 quadrants)
Bitemporal hemianopia: chiasm (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma)
Homonymous hemianopia: contralateral tract, radiations or occipital lobe (stroke, tumour); macular sparing = occipital
img: Endocrine work-up (prolactin, GH, ACTH…) if pituitary
tx: Treat the cause: dopamine agonist (prolactinoma), transsphenoidal surgery, stroke management
oth: Quadrantanopia: temporal lobe = superior ("pie in the sky"), parietal = inferior
paths.def: Visual field defects localise the lesion along the visual pathway: monocular (retina/optic nerve), bitemporal (chiasm), homonymous (tract → cortex).

sx: Congenital: often unnoticed, discovered at school/medical exam
Acquired: dull colours, red desaturation (optic neuritis)
ex: Congenital: bilateral, symmetrical, stable, mostly MALES (8 %) – protan (red), deutan (green), tritan (blue, rare, autosomal)
Acquired: unilateral/asymmetric, progressive; optic nerve → red-green, retina/macula → blue-yellow
lab: Anomaloscope (Nagel – matching, diagnosis of anomalous trichromacy)
tx: Congenital: no treatment (counselling, career)
Acquired: treat the cause; may improve
oth: Protanopia = cannot see red; deuteranopia = green; tritanopia = blue
paths.def: Abnormal colour perception: congenital (X-linked cone pigment defects) or acquired (retina, optic nerve, drugs).

sx: Blurred distance vision, squinting; near vision good
Floaters/flashes in high myopia (RD risk)
ex: VA improves with pinhole and minus lenses
High myopia (> −6 D): tilted disc, peripapillary atrophy, posterior staphyloma, lacquer cracks, Fuchs spot, lattice
lab: Refraction (cycloplegic in children), keratometry, axial length (biometry)
tx: Divergent (concave, minus) glasses or contact lenses
Refractive surgery (LASIK, PRK, phakic IOL) when stable
Myopia control in children: low-dose atropine, outdoor time, special lenses
cx: Rhegmatogenous RD, myopic CNV/maculopathy, open-angle glaucoma, early nuclear cataract, amblyopia if anisometropic
oth: Presbyopia appears LATER in myopes
paths.def: Refractive error in which parallel rays focus IN FRONT of the retina (axial – long eye – or refractive).

sx: Near vision blurred first, asthenopia (headache, eye strain), early presbyopia
Children: accommodative esotropia, amblyopia
ex: Small eye, crowded disc (pseudopapilloedema), shallow AC (angle-closure risk)
tx: Convergent (convex, plus) lenses – full correction in accommodative esotropia
oth: Latent vs manifest hyperopia; total revealed by cycloplegia
paths.def: Refractive error in which parallel rays focus BEHIND the retina (short eye); compensated by accommodation in the young.

sx: Astigmatism: blurred/distorted vision at all distances, asthenopia
Presbyopia (≥ 40–45 y): needs to hold text farther away, worse in dim light
ex: Keratometry/topography (regular vs irregular – keratoconus)
tx: Astigmatism: cylindrical (toric) lenses, rigid contact lenses, toric IOL
Anisometropia: contact lenses, amblyopia treatment in children
Presbyopia: plus lenses for near (reading, bifocal, progressive)
oth: Presbyopia: earlier in hyperopes, later in myopes
paths.def: Astigmatism = different refractive power along the meridians; anisometropia = refraction difference between eyes; presbyopia = physiological loss of accommodation with age.

sx: Visible squint, no diplopia (suppression), abnormal head posture rarely
ex: Hirschberg corneal reflex, cover test (tropia), alternate cover (total deviation)
Esotropia (often accommodative, hyperopia) or exotropia
Full motility
lab: Cycloplegic refraction, VA each eye (amblyopia), fundus (exclude retinoblastoma, cataract)
tx: 1 Glasses (full hyperopic correction) → 2 occlusion of the good eye for amblyopia → 3 orthoptics → 4 surgery (recession/resection) in childhood
oth: Always examine the fundus of a child with squint (retinoblastoma)
paths.def: Manifest deviation of one eye with the same angle in all directions of gaze, usually starting in childhood.

sx: Sudden DIPLOPIA (binocular, disappears with one eye covered), vertigo, false projection (past-pointing)
Compensatory head posture
ex: Limited movement and maximal deviation in the field of the paralysed muscle; secondary deviation > primary
III: ptosis, eye down & out, mydriasis; IV: hypertropia, head tilt; VI: esotropia, no abduction
lab: Diabetes, BP, ESR/CRP (> 50 y), myasthenia tests (ice test, antibodies)
img: Urgent CT/MR angiography for pupil-involving III palsy (posterior communicating aneurysm)
tx: Treat the cause; occlusion or prisms for diplopia; botulinum toxin; surgery after 6–12 months of stability
oth: Diplopia worse looking to the right = right VI (or left III medial rectus)
paths.def: Deviation due to paralysis of an extraocular muscle or its nerve; incomitant (angle varies with gaze).

sx: Often asymptomatic – detected by screening
ex: Reduced VA of one eye despite correction, crowding phenomenon
lab: VA each eye (picture charts), cycloplegic refraction, cover test, red reflex/fundus
tx: Remove the cause (cataract surgery, ptosis surgery, glasses)
Occlusion (patching) or atropine penalisation of the GOOD eye
Treat before strabismus surgery
oth: Types: strabismic, anisometropic, deprivation (worst), ametropic (bilateral)
paths.def: Unilateral (rarely bilateral) decrease of best-corrected VA without organic lesion, caused by abnormal visual experience during the sensitive period (< 7–8 years).

sx: Fever, pain, red swollen lids, decreased VA in severe cases
ex: PROPTOSIS, painful and limited eye movements, chemosis, ± RAPD
Preseptal: lid swelling WITHOUT proptosis, normal motility and VA
tx: Hospitalisation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, ENT consult, drainage of subperiosteal/orbital abscess or sinus
cx: Optic neuropathy, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess
oth: Children: ethmoiditis is the commonest cause
paths.def: Acute infection of the orbital soft tissues behind the orbital septum, mostly from ethmoid sinusitis.

sx: Gritty eyes, tearing, staring look, diplopia, decreased VA/colour (optic neuropathy)
ex: Upper lid retraction (Dalrymple) – most frequent, lid lag (von Graefe), Kocher (staring), proptosis
Restrictive myopathy (inferior & medial rectus), exposure keratopathy, conjunctival injection over muscles
img: CT/MRI orbit: enlarged muscle BELLIES sparing tendons
tx: Stop smoking, restore euthyroidism, lubricants, selenium (mild)
Active moderate-severe: IV methylprednisolone, teprotumumab, orbital radiotherapy
Optic neuropathy: IV steroids ± urgent decompression; later strabismus & lid surgery
oth: Radioiodine can worsen TED (steroid cover)
paths.def: Autoimmune inflammation of orbital fat and extraocular muscles, most common cause of uni/bilateral exophthalmos in adults.

sx: Painless progressive proptosis, diplopia, decreased VA (compression)
Myositis: pain worse on eye movement
ex: Axial (intraconal) or displaced proptosis, palpable mass, disc oedema/folds
tx: Surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy according to type
Myositis: systemic corticosteroids
oth: Children: capillary haemangioma, dermoid cyst, rhabdomyosarcoma (fast!)
Adults: cavernous haemangioma, lymphoma, meningioma, metastases
paths.def: Space-occupying lesions causing progressive proptosis; myositis = idiopathic inflammation of extraocular muscles.

sx: Epiphora, sticky eye, crusting
ex: Reflux of mucopus from the puncta on pressure over the sac; quiet eye, normal cornea
tx: Massage of the sac (Crigler) + topical antibiotics; most resolve by 1 year
PROBING of the nasolacrimal duct = treatment of choice if persistent
oth: DDx: congenital glaucoma (photophobia, big cloudy cornea), gonococcal conjunctivitis
paths.def: Imperforate valve of Hasner causing epiphora and mucopurulent discharge from the first weeks of life.

sx: Acute: painful red swelling at the medial canthus, epiphora
Chronic: epiphora + mucopurulent discharge
ex: Swelling BELOW the medial canthal tendon, reflux of pus on pressure
tx: Acute: systemic antibiotics, warm compresses, abscess drainage
Definitive: dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR)
cx: Orbital cellulitis, lacrimal fistula, endophthalmitis after intraocular surgery
oth: Treat chronic dacryocystitis before cataract surgery
paths.def: Infection of the lacrimal sac secondary to nasolacrimal duct obstruction.

sx: Dry eye: burning, grittiness, worse in the evening/screens
Dacryoadenitis: pain and swelling of the upper-outer lid
ex: Reduced tear meniscus, punctate staining (fluorescein/lissamine)
Dacryoadenitis: S-shaped ptosis, tender gland, pre-auricular nodes
img: Orbit CT/MRI for chronic dacryoadenitis (sarcoid, lymphoma)
tx: Artificial tears, lid hygiene, omega-3, cyclosporine, punctal plugs
Dacryoadenitis: viral – supportive; bacterial – antibiotics; inflammatory – steroids
oth: Causes of dry eye: age, Sjögren, MGD/blepharitis, drugs, screen use
paths.def: Dry eye = tear film insufficiency/instability; dacryoadenitis = inflammation of the lacrimal gland.

sx: Bilateral burning, itching, grittiness, worse in the MORNING, crusts
ex: Red thickened margins, scales/collarettes, telangiectasia, plugged meibomian orifices, madarosis/trichiasis
tx: Warm compresses + lid massage + lid hygiene (cornerstone, long-term)
Topical antibiotic (staph), oral doxycycline/azithromycin (MGD, rosacea), short weak steroids
cx: Chalazion, hordeolum, dry eye, marginal keratitis, chronic conjunctivitis
oth: Associated with seborrhoeic dermatitis and rosacea
paths.def: Chronic inflammation of the eyelid margins (anterior: staphylococcal/seborrhoeic/Demodex; posterior: meibomian gland dysfunction).

sx: Chalazion: painless lump
Hordeolum: painful red swelling
ex: Chalazion: firm nodule away from the margin
External hordeolum: pointing at the lash base (Zeis); internal: meibomian
lab: Histology if recurrent at the same site (sebaceous carcinoma)
tx: Warm compresses, lid hygiene
Chalazion: incision & curettage (or steroid injection)
Hordeolum: compresses, topical antibiotic, drainage if needed
cx: Preseptal cellulitis (hordeolum), astigmatism from large chalazion
oth: Recurrent chalazia → chronic blepharitis, rosacea
paths.def: Chalazion = chronic sterile lipogranuloma of a meibomian gland; hordeolum = acute staphylococcal abscess of a lid gland.

sx: Entropion: foreign-body sensation, red eye
Ectropion: epiphora, irritation
ex: Entropion: lashes rubbing the cornea, punctate erosions/ulcer
Ectropion: everted lower lid, exposed conjunctiva/punctum
tx: Surgery (involutional, cicatricial); lubricants; taping
Paralytic: lubrication, taping, gold weight, tarsorrhaphy
oth: Entropion: involutional, cicatricial (trachoma, chemical burn), spastic, congenital
Ectropion: involutional, paralytic (VII), cicatricial, mechanical, spastic
paths.def: Malpositions of the lid margin: inward (entropion) or outward (ectropion); lagophthalmos = incomplete closure.

sx: Ptosis: obstructed superior field; tumour: painless growing lesion
ex: Ptosis: levator function, MRD1, fatigability (myasthenia), pupil (III/Horner)
BCC: pearly nodule with telangiectasia, central ulcer, lower lid/medial canthus
lab: Biopsy of suspicious lesions; myasthenia tests
tx: Ptosis surgery (levator advancement, frontalis sling)
Tumours: excision with margin control (Mohs)
cx: Congenital ptosis covering the pupil → amblyopia
oth: Malignant: BCC > SCC > sebaceous carcinoma (mimics chalazion) > melanoma
paths.def: Ptosis = drooping upper lid; most frequent malignant lid tumour = basal cell carcinoma.

sx: Red eye, watery discharge, grittiness, starts in one eye then the other, recent cold/fever
ex: Follicles, tender PRE-AURICULAR lymph node, ± pseudomembranes, subepithelial corneal infiltrates
tx: Hygiene, cold compresses, artificial tears; antibiotics useless
Steroids only for membranes/infiltrates reducing VA
cx: Very contagious 2 weeks – hand washing, disinfect instruments
oth: VA normal unless corneal infiltrates
paths.def: Most frequent infectious conjunctivitis (~80 %): epidemic keratoconjunctivitis or pharyngoconjunctival fever.

sx: Mucopurulent discharge, lids stuck in the morning
ex: Papillae, diffuse superficial congestion; gonococcal: hyperpurulent, chemosis, lid oedema
lab: Gram stain/culture in severe and neonatal cases (intracellular diplococci, chlamydial inclusions)
tx: Wash secretions, broad-spectrum antibiotic drops
Neonatal: HOSPITALISE + systemic antibiotics (ceftriaxone for gonococcus, erythromycin for chlamydia)
Prophylaxis at birth: erythromycin/povidone-iodine (historically AgNO3 – Credé)
cx: Gonococcal keratitis with perforation; chlamydial pneumonia
oth: Timing: chemical day 1, gonococcal day 2–4, chlamydial day 5–14
paths.def: Infection by staphylococci, streptococci, Haemophilus; in neonates gonococcus, chlamydia.

sx: ITCHING (key), watery discharge, bilateral, seasonal (spring)
ex: Chemosis, papillae; vernal/GPC: giant cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsus, Trantas dots; contact-lens overwear
tx: Avoid allergen, cold compresses, antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops (olopatadine, ketotifen)
Short courses of topical steroids (watch IOP, cataract); cyclosporine in vernal; stop contact lenses
oth: No antibiotics
paths.def: IgE-mediated (type I) conjunctival reaction, often with rhinitis.

sx: Normal VA + discomfort = conjunctivitis; decreased VA + pain = keratitis / uveitis / acute glaucoma
ex: Superficial (peripheral) congestion → conjunctivitis
Ciliary (perikeratic) injection → keratitis, iridocyclitis, acute glaucoma
Pupil: miosis (uveitis), mid-dilated fixed (acute glaucoma); cornea: stain (keratitis), oedema (glaucoma)
tx: Refer urgently any red eye with decreased vision or severe pain
cx: Scleritis (deep violaceous, boring pain), subconjunctival haemorrhage (painless, normal VA)
oth: Never steroids without slit-lamp examination (HSV)
paths.def: Systematic approach: congestion type, vision, pain, pupil, cornea, IOP.

sx: Unilateral red eye, pain, photophobia, tearing, blurred vision, recurrent episodes
ex: Dendritic ulcer staining with fluorescein (terminal bulbs); geographic ulcer; DECREASED corneal sensation
Disciform: stromal oedema, intact epithelium, KP
tx: Epithelial: topical aciclovir ointment 5×/d or ganciclovir gel, debridement, cycloplegic – NO STEROIDS
Stromal: antiviral cover + topical steroids
Recurrent: oral aciclovir prophylaxis 400 mg ×2
cx: Stromal scarring (leucoma), neurotrophic ulcer, perforation, uveitis, glaucoma
oth: Steroids on an epithelial dendrite → geographic ulcer
paths.def: Reactivation of latent HSV-1 (trigeminal ganglion) along corneal nerves; epithelial (dendritic) or stromal (disciform).

sx: Prodromal hemicranial pain, then vesicular rash (forehead, upper lid, nose) not crossing the midline
ex: Hutchinson sign (nasociliary – tip of nose) → eye involvement: conjunctivitis, pseudodendrites, keratitis, uveitis, ± III palsy
tx: Oral aciclovir 800 mg ×5/d (or valaciclovir) for 7–10 days within 72 h, analgesics
Topical steroids for stromal keratitis/uveitis
oth: Risk factors: elderly, AIDS, diabetes, immunosuppressive therapy
paths.def: VZV reactivation in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve.

sx: Pain, redness, photophobia, decreased VA, discharge
ex: White stromal infiltrate with epithelial defect, purulent discharge, HYPOPYON
Fungal: feathery borders, satellite lesions (plant trauma); Acanthamoeba: severe pain, ring infiltrate (contact lens + water)
lab: Corneal scraping: Gram, culture, antibiogram; contact lens & case culture
tx: Intensive hourly fortified antibiotics or fluoroquinolone; cycloplegic
Fungal: natamycin/voriconazole; Acanthamoeba: PHMB/chlorhexidine
Steroids only later, under control
oth: Risk factors: contact lenses, trauma, dry eye, entropion/trichiasis, chronic dacryocystitis, immunosuppression
paths.def: Microbial keratitis: requires an epithelial break (except gonococcus); emergency.

sx: Exposure: irritation; neurotrophic: few symptoms; keratoconus: progressive blur; scleritis: severe deep boring pain
ex: Exposure: inferior punctate erosions (lagophthalmos)
Neurotrophic: persistent epithelial defect, anaesthetic cornea (V lesion, HSV)
Keratoconus: Munson sign, Vogt striae, Fleischer ring
Scleritis: violaceous deep injection, tender
tx: Exposure: lubricants, taping, tarsorrhaphy
Keratoconus: rigid lenses, cross-linking, keratoplasty
Scleritis: systemic NSAIDs/steroids/immunosuppression
oth: Episcleritis: benign, sectoral, mild
paths.def: Non-infectious corneal and scleral disorders.

sx: Pain, photophobia, redness, blurred vision, tearing
ex: Ciliary injection, MIOSIS, KP, flare & cells, hypopyon, posterior synechiae (irregular pupil), IOP ↓ or ↑
lab: If recurrent/bilateral: HLA-B27, chest X-ray (sarcoid, TB), syphilis serology, ACE
tx: Topical steroids (dexamethasone/prednisolone) + mydriatic-cycloplegic (atropine/tropicamide/phenylephrine)
Treat cause; systemic therapy if severe/recurrent
cx: Posterior synechiae, complicated cataract, secondary glaucoma, band keratopathy, CME
oth: DDx: conjunctivitis (normal VA, superficial congestion), keratitis, acute glaucoma
paths.def: Inflammation of the iris ± ciliary body.

sx: Floaters, blurred vision, usually white painless eye
ex: Vitreous cells, snowballs; toxoplasma: white fluffy retinochoroiditis next to a pigmented scar; CMV, ARN in immunosuppressed
tx: Toxoplasmosis (threatening macula/optic disc): pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid + steroids, or cotrimoxazole
Non-infectious: steroids, immunosuppressants
oth: Congenital toxoplasmosis → bilateral macular scars, low vision
paths.def: Inflammation of the vitreous/pars plana (intermediate) or choroid/retina (posterior).

sx: Endophthalmitis: pain, decreased VA days after surgery/trauma
ex: Hypopyon, vitritis, lid oedema, reduced red reflex
tx: Intravitreal vancomycin + ceftazidime, ± vitrectomy
Sympathetic ophthalmia: systemic steroids/immunosuppressants
oth: Causes: cataract surgery, penetrating injury (IOFB), endogenous (septicaemia), perforated ulcer
paths.def: Endophthalmitis = intraocular infection; sympathetic ophthalmia = bilateral granulomatous uveitis after injury to one eye.

sx: Progressive painless blurring, glare, poor night vision, monocular diplopia, myopic shift (nuclear: "second sight")
ex: Lens opacity at slit lamp, dark opacities against the red reflex, leukocoria (mature)
Pinhole may not improve
lab: Biometry (axial length, keratometry) for IOL power, B-scan if no fundus view
tx: Phacoemulsification + foldable posterior chamber IOL when vision limits daily life
cx: Intumescent → phacomorphic glaucoma; hypermature → phacolytic glaucoma, phaco-anaphylactic uveitis, lens luxation
oth: Risk factors: age, diabetes, smoking, UV, steroids
paths.def: Progressive opacification of the lens with age: nuclear, cortical, posterior subcapsular.

sx: Child: leukocoria, strabismus, nystagmus (bilateral)
ex: Zonular (lamellar) = most frequent congenital; rosette = contusion; sunflower = Wilson/copper
lab: Congenital: TORCH (rubella), galactosaemia, Lowe; metabolic: glucose, calcium
tx: Dense congenital cataract: surgery within weeks + optical correction + amblyopia treatment
oth: Complicated: chronic uveitis, high myopia, RP, glaucoma, RD, tumours; drugs: steroids
paths.def: Non-senile cataracts with specific causes.

paths.n: Lens subluxation/luxation & aphakia; cataract surgery complications
sx: Monocular diplopia, fluctuating vision; anterior luxation → acute painful glaucoma
ex: Iridodonesis, phacodonesis, unequal AC depth, vitreous in AC, lens edge in the pupil
tx: Lensectomy/vitrectomy with IOL; aphakia: IOL, contact lens, glasses
cx: Surgery: endophthalmitis, posterior capsule rupture, CME, RD, PCO ("secondary cataract" → YAG capsulotomy)
oth: Marfan: up and out; homocystinuria: down and in
paths.def: Displacement of the lens from the zonular support; aphakia = absence of the lens.

ex: Digital tonometry: rough estimate (rock-hard eye in acute glaucoma)
lab: Goldmann applanation (gold standard), air-puff, Schiøtz, rebound
tx: Lowering drugs: prostaglandins, β-blockers, CAIs, α2-agonists, pilocarpine, osmotics
oth: Diurnal variation > 5 mmHg is pathological
paths.def: IOP results from aqueous production (ciliary processes) vs outflow (trabeculum – Schlemm; uveoscleral). Normal 10–21 mmHg.

sx: ASYMPTOMATIC, painless; late tunnel vision
ex: Enlarged vertical cup (C/D > 0.6, asymmetry > 0.2), rim notching, disc haemorrhage
IOP > 21 (or normal-tension)
img: Visual field: paracentral, arcuate (Bjerrum), nasal step
OCT RNFL – detects damage years before VF
tx: Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost) → β-blockers, CAIs, α2 → SLT laser → trabeculectomy/tubes
Lifelong follow-up
oth: Risk factors: age, IOP, family history, black ethnicity, myopia, thin cornea
paths.def: Chronic progressive optic neuropathy with open angle, usually raised IOP, characteristic VF loss.

sx: Severe pain, hemicrania, nausea/vomiting, blurred vision, coloured haloes
ex: Red eye, corneal oedema, fixed mid-dilated vertically oval pupil, shallow AC, IOP 50–80, rock-hard globe
tx: IV acetazolamide + mannitol, topical β-blocker, steroids, pilocarpine when IOP lower
LASER PERIPHERAL IRIDOTOMY both eyes; lens extraction if narrow angle persists; trabeculectomy if IOP stays high
cx: Optic atrophy, glaukomflecken, iris atrophy, chronic angle closure
oth: Risk: hyperopia, female, elderly, mydriasis (drugs, darkness)
paths.def: Sudden closure of a narrow angle (pupillary block) with very high IOP.

sx: Congenital: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm
ex: Buphthalmos, corneal diameter > 12 mm, cloudy cornea, Haab striae, cupping
Neovascular: rubeosis iridis, very high IOP, painful
tx: Congenital: SURGERY (goniotomy/trabeculotomy)
Neovascular: anti-VEGF + PRP + IOP control
Phacomorphic/phacolytic: cataract surgery
Uveitic: steroids + cycloplegics; steroid-induced: stop steroid
oth: Secondary: neovascular, lens-induced, uveitic, steroid, traumatic, pigmentary, pseudoexfoliation
paths.def: Congenital = angle dysgenesis; secondary = identifiable cause.

sx: Sudden painless near-total monocular blindness (seconds), amaurosis fugax before
ex: Pale white retina, CHERRY-RED SPOT, thin segmented arteries, embolus (Hollenhorst), RAPD
tx: Emergency: ocular massage, lower IOP (acetazolamide, paracentesis) – limited benefit; treat GCA with steroids; stroke prevention
oth: Poor visual prognosis; equivalent of a stroke
paths.def: Embolic or thrombotic (or arteritic) occlusion of the central retinal artery → inner retinal infarction.

sx: Sudden or subacute painless blurred vision (BRVO: sectoral)
ex: Flame haemorrhages (4 quadrants in CRVO), dilated tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots, disc & macular oedema
lab: BP, glucose, lipids, IOP (glaucoma risk factor), thrombophilia if young
tx: Intravitreal anti-VEGF or dexamethasone implant for macular oedema
PRP if neovascularisation (ischaemic)
Control risk factors
cx: Macular oedema, neovascular glaucoma ("100-day glaucoma"), vitreous haemorrhage
oth: Risk factors: age, hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma
paths.def: Thrombosis of the central or a branch retinal vein, often at an AV crossing.

sx: Asymptomatic for long; decreased VA (macular oedema), floaters/sudden loss (vitreous haemorrhage)
ex: NPDR: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA
PDR: neovessels on disc/elsewhere/iris
tx: Glycaemic/BP control; anti-VEGF for centre-involving DME; PRP for PDR; vitrectomy for non-clearing haemorrhage/tractional RD
Screening: type 2 at diagnosis, type 1 after 5 years, then yearly
cx: Vitreous haemorrhage, TRACTIONAL RD, neovascular glaucoma, cataract
oth: Main cause of blindness in working-age adults
paths.def: Microangiopathy of the retina: non-proliferative → proliferative; maculopathy at any stage.

sx: Central vision loss, difficulty reading/recognising faces, METAMORPHOPSIA (wet), central scotoma; peripheral vision preserved
ex: Drusen, pigment changes; dry: geographic atrophy; wet: CNV, subretinal haemorrhage/fluid
tx: Wet: intravitreal anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, faricimab) – repeated
Dry: AREDS antioxidants/zinc, stop smoking, low-vision aids
oth: Risk factors: age, smoking (main modifiable), genetics, family history
paths.def: Degenerative disease of the macula (RPE–Bruch–choriocapillaris) after 50 years.

sx: Floaters (myodesopsia), flashes (photopsia), progressive "curtain" field defect, VA loss when macula detaches
ex: Grey elevated mobile retina with a break (horseshoe tear), Shafer sign (pigment in vitreous)
tx: Surgery: vitrectomy + gas/silicone, scleral buckle, pneumatic retinopexy; laser/cryo for tears without detachment
Macula-on = emergency
oth: Risk: high myopia, lattice, PVD, cataract surgery, trauma, fellow-eye RD
paths.def: Separation of the neurosensory retina from the RPE: rhegmatogenous (break), tractional, exudative.

sx: RB: leukocoria, strabismus, red painful eye (late)
Melanoma: often asymptomatic, blurred vision, field defect
ex: RB: white retinal mass, calcifications, seeding
Melanoma: elevated brown (or amelanotic) mushroom-shaped mass, orange pigment, exudative RD
img: Ultrasound (RB calcifications; melanoma low internal reflectivity), MRI
tx: RB: chemotherapy (IV/intra-arterial), laser, cryo, brachytherapy, enucleation
Melanoma: brachytherapy/proton therapy, enucleation for large tumours
oth: Naevus: flat, < 2 mm, drusen on surface – monitor
paths.def: Retinoblastoma = most frequent malignant intraocular tumour of childhood; choroidal melanoma = most frequent primary in adults.

sx: RP: night blindness, tunnel vision
ex: RP: bone-spicule pigmentation, attenuated arterioles, waxy pale disc
HT: arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, exudates, disc oedema (malignant)
tx: RP: low-vision aids, gene therapy (RPE65), cataract surgery
HT: control BP
oth: Keith–Wagener–Barker grades I–IV
paths.def: RP = inherited rod–cone dystrophy; hypertensive retinopathy = retinal vascular changes of high BP.

sx: Subacute monocular VA loss over days, PAIN on eye movement, faded colours
ex: RAPD, red desaturation, central/centro-caecal scotoma
Retrobulbar: NORMAL disc; papillitis: swollen hyperaemic disc
tx: IV methylprednisolone 1 g/d × 3 days then oral taper (faster recovery)
Disease-modifying therapy for MS
oth: Good spontaneous recovery in most
paths.def: Inflammatory demyelinating optic neuropathy, often associated with multiple sclerosis.

sx: Sudden PAINLESS monocular loss, often on waking; GCA: headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, PMR
ex: Swollen (pale in GCA) disc, splinter haemorrhages, ALTITUDINAL (inferior) field defect, RAPD
tx: GCA: immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (protect the other eye)
NAION: control risk factors, aspirin
cx: Optic atrophy; GCA: bilateral blindness, CRAO
oth: NAION risk: small crowded disc ("disc at risk"), HT, diabetes, sleep apnoea
paths.def: Infarction of the optic nerve head (short posterior ciliary arteries): non-arteritic or arteritic (giant cell arteritis).

sx: Papilloedema: headache, nausea, transient visual obscurations, VA preserved long
ex: Papilloedema: blurred elevated margins, venous engorgement, haemorrhages, enlarged blind spot
Atrophy: pale/white disc, RAPD, VA/colour loss
tx: Treat cause (tumour, IIH: weight loss, acetazolamide, shunt)
oth: Causes of bilateral papilloedema: tumours, hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis), IIH, SAH, venous sinus thrombosis
paths.def: Papilloedema = bilateral disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure; optic atrophy = loss of optic nerve fibres (pale disc).

sx: Usually asymptomatic; anisocoria
ex: RAPD (swinging flashlight)
Amaurotic rigidity: blind eye, no direct, consensual preserved
Absolute rigidity: III lesion, no direct nor consensual
Horner: miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis; Adie; Argyll Robertson
img: Horner: imaging of the sympathetic chain (carotid dissection, Pancoast)
tx: Treat cause
oth: Anisocoria greater in the light = efferent parasympathetic (III, Adie); greater in the dark = Horner
paths.def: Afferent (optic nerve/retina) vs efferent (III, sympathetic) defects.

sx: Severe pain, blepharospasm, decreased vision
ex: Epithelial defect, limbal ischaemia (white blanching = severe), corneal haze
Grading by limbal ischaemia and corneal opacity
tx: IMMEDIATE copious irrigation (water, saline, ≥ 30 min, until pH 7), remove particles, evert lids
Then antibiotics, cycloplegics, steroids (first week), vitamin C, doxycycline, amniotic membrane
cx: Symblepharon, vascularised leucoma, dry eye, glaucoma, limbal stem cell deficiency
oth: Do NOT neutralise – irrigate
paths.def: Alkali (lime, ammonia, NaOH – liquefaction, deep penetration) or acid (coagulation, more superficial) injuries.

sx: Pain, decreased VA, diplopia (blow-out)
ex: Hyphaema, traumatic mydriasis, iridodialysis (D-shaped pupil), angle recession, lens subluxation, commotio retinae (Berlin oedema), choroidal rupture, retinal tears, vitreous haemorrhage, optic nerve avulsion
tx: Hyphaema: rest, head elevation, topical steroids + cycloplegics, IOP control, avoid aspirin/NSAIDs; washout if blood staining/raised IOP
cx: Rebleeding, corneal blood staining (most serious), glaucoma (early & angle recession late), cataract, RD
oth: Hyphaema = blood with horizontal level in AC
paths.def: Closed-globe injury with anteroposterior compression and equatorial expansion.

paths.n: Open globe injury & intraocular foreign body
sx: Pain, decreased vision, history of hammering/metal
ex: Irregular/peaked pupil, shallow AC, uveal prolapse, positive Seidel test, hypotony
img: CT orbit (IOFB) – MRI contraindicated if metallic
tx: Rigid shield, no pressure/drops, nil by mouth, tetanus, IV antibiotics → urgent watertight repair
Metallic IOFB: always remove (vitrectomy)
cx: Endophthalmitis, sympathetic ophthalmia, siderosis (iron), chalcosis (copper), RD
oth: Corneal foreign body: removal at slit lamp; under upper lid → vertical scratches
paths.def: Full-thickness wound of cornea/sclera (penetrating or perforating), ± IOFB.

questions.q: The congenital defects of color vision:

o.t: Appear most frequently in elder patients

questions.note: Congenital colour vision defects cannot be treated (neither medically nor surgically), are bilateral and symmetrical, and are present from birth (not acquired with age).

questions.q: The rod cells present the following characters:

o.t: are located in the peripheral retina
they are responsible for the day vision
they are responsible for the night vision

questions.note: Rods: peripheral retina, night (scotopic) vision, contain rhodopsin. Cones: macula, day/colour vision, iodopsin.

questions.q: The congenital defects of color vision:
questions.note: Congenital colour defects are X-linked recessive → mostly males (≈ 8 % of men, 0.5 % of women); untreatable, bilateral, symmetrical.

questions.q: Protanopy is a colour disturbance meaning that the patient can not see at all:
questions.note: Protanopia = absence of red (L) cones; deuteranopia = green; tritanopia = blue.

questions.q: Narrowing of the visual field appears in:
questions.note: Visual field constriction/defects: optic atrophy, chiasmal compression (pituitary tumour, meningioma), RP (concentric), advanced glaucoma (tubular), retinal detachment (sector). Optic neuritis gives a CENTRAL scotoma.

questions.q: For the examination of visual acuity we need:
questions.note: Distance VA is measured with an optotype (Snellen chart) at 5–6 m (+ near chart, pinhole).

questions.q: The examination of the visual field is made by:
questions.note: Visual field: perimetry (Goldmann kinetic, Humphrey static), campimetry (central field) and the confrontation test.

questions.q: The visual pathway, after leaving the eyeball, is made of:
questions.note: Visual pathway: optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → optic radiations → occipital (calcarine) visual cortex.

questions.q: In heteronymous hemianopsia the lesion is located
questions.note: Heteronymous (bitemporal) hemianopia = chiasmal lesion. Retrochiasmal lesions (tract, radiations, cortex) give homonymous defects.

questions.q: Cycloplegia is made with:
questions.note: Cycloplegia: atropine (long-acting, children), cyclopentolate, tropicamide (short). Pilocarpine is a miotic that STIMULATES accommodation.

questions.q: The rod cells present the following characteristics

o.t: Are located in the peripherial retina
They are responsible for the day vision

questions.note: Rods: peripheral retina, night vision, rhodopsin.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Visual acuity measured in clinic depends on:
questions.note: Clinical VA depends on the macula (fovea) and its cones.

questions.q: The endocrinology team refers a patient with a pituitary tumour who complains of visual field problems. Which type of visual field defect do you expect?
questions.note: A pituitary adenoma compresses the optic chiasm (crossing nasal fibres) → bitemporal hemianopia. Altitudinal defects are typical of AION. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Visual acuity depends mostly on:
questions.note: Of the options, only the ganglion cells (the macular cone → bipolar → ganglion cell pathway, 1:1 ratio in the fovea) carry central high-resolution vision. Rods and the peripheral retina serve night and peripheral vision. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Visual acuity depends on:
questions.note: Central visual acuity is provided by the foveal cones. Rods (peripheral retina) serve scotopic and peripheral vision; ciliary processes produce aqueous humour; the ora serrata is the anterior limit of the retina. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Congenital colour vision defects are:
questions.note: Congenital dyschromatopsias (X-linked red–green, mostly in males) are bilateral, symmetrical, stable and untreatable. Acquired defects are asymmetrical, progressive and may improve with treatment of the cause. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Bitemporal hemianopia appears in:

o.t: A lesion in the left cerebral hemisphere
A lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere

questions.note: Chiasmal compression (pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma) → bitemporal hemianopia. Retrochiasmal lesions → contralateral homonymous hemianopia; RP → concentric constriction. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Left homonymous hemianopia appears in:

o.t: A lesion in the left cerebral hemisphere
A lesion in the right cerebral hemisphere

questions.note: Retrochiasmal lesions give a CONTRALATERAL homonymous hemianopia: a left hemianopia = right optic tract / radiation / occipital cortex lesion. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Acquired colour vision defects are:
questions.note: Acquired dyschromatopsias (optic neuropathies → red–green; retinal/macular diseases → blue–yellow) are often unilateral or asymmetrical, progressive and may recover when the cause is treated. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Roles of the cones:
questions.note: Cones (macula/fovea): photopic (day) vision, high visual acuity and colour vision. Rods: scotopic (night) and peripheral vision. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In a hyperopic eye the focus is localized:
questions.note: Hyperopia: parallel rays focus BEHIND the retina (short eye or weak dioptric power) → convergent lenses.

questions.q: The following statements about presbyopia are FALSE, except one:

o.t: It is a pathologic decrease in the amplitude of accommodation associated with aging
It is a physiological trouble of accommodation
Symptoms: normal near vision and blurred vision at distance

questions.note: Presbyopia is a PHYSIOLOGICAL age-related loss of accommodation (≈ 40–45 y): blurred NEAR vision with normal distance vision, corrected by convex (convergent) lenses.

questions.q: Correction of myopia is performed with:
questions.note: Myopia → spherical divergent (concave, minus) lenses.

questions.q: In a myopic eye the focus is localised:
questions.note: Myopia: focus in front of the retina.

questions.q: Correction of the hyperopia is made with:
questions.note: Hyperopia → spherical convergent (convex, plus) lenses.

questions.q: Correction of presbiopia is made with:
questions.note: Presbyopia → convergent (plus) lenses for near.

questions.q: Correction of astigmatism is made with:
questions.note: Astigmatism → cylindrical (toric) lenses, or rigid contact lenses.

questions.q: In hyperopic eyes presbyopia manifests:
questions.note: Hyperopes already use part of their accommodation for distance → presbyopia appears EARLIER; myopes later.

questions.q: The possible complications in high myopia are:
questions.note: High myopia: vitreous degeneration/liquefaction, lattice → retinal detachment, myopic maculopathy (CNV → haemorrhage), early nuclear cataract, glaucoma.

questions.q: In myopia the image is formed:
questions.note: Myopia: image in front of the retina.

questions.q: Accomodative asthenopia appears most frequently in:
questions.note: Accommodative asthenopia (eye strain) is typical of uncorrected hyperopia (and astigmatism): constant accommodative effort.

questions.q: Accommodative asthenopia appears in patients with:
questions.note: Accommodative asthenopia: hyperopia and astigmatism (also presbyopia not corrected).

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: All of these statements concerning myopia are correct, EXCEPT:

o.t: In distant vision the rays converge in front of the retina
The anteroposterior axis of the eye is smaller than in the emmetropic subject
It must be corrected with a concave lens
Visual acuity remains good in close vision without optical correction

questions.note: EXCEPT: in axial myopia the antero-posterior axis is LONGER than in emmetropia. The others are true (focus in front, progresses in adolescence, concave lens, good near vision).

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: A 30 year old patient does not see well when reading. The probable refractive error will most likely be:
questions.note: At 30, near difficulty is most likely latent hyperopia (accommodation insufficient for near); presbyopia starts ≈ 40–45 y.

questions.q: Convergent spherical lenses are used to correct:
questions.note: Convergent (plus) spherical lenses: hyperopia, presbyopia, aphakia.

questions.q: Pathological disorders of dynamic refraction include:
questions.note: Dynamic refraction = accommodation; its disorders: presbyopia (physiological loss), accommodative paralysis/spasm. Ametropias (astigmatism, anisometropia) are static refraction disorders.

questions.q: In case of myopia, the following are true:

o.t: Progression with age is not possible
The pinhole test observes improvement in distance visual acuity

questions.note: Myopia: corrected with divergent lenses (glasses or contact lenses), good near vision, presbyopia appears LATER, may progress (school myopia, pathological myopia); pinhole improves distance VA.

questions.q: Cylindrical lenses can be used to correct:
questions.note: Cylindrical (toric) lenses correct astigmatism only; presbyopia needs convergent spherical lenses, anisometropia is corrected by spherical lenses/contact lenses. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 30-year-old patient does not see well when reading. Possible refractive problems are:
questions.note: At 30, presbyopia has not started (≈ 40–45 y). A hyperope uses accommodation permanently → near difficulties and accommodative asthenopia; astigmatism blurs at all distances. A myope sees well at near. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: High myopia can be complicated by:
questions.note: Pathological myopia: lattice degeneration and retinal tears → rhegmatogenous RD, myopic maculopathy (CNV, Fuchs spot, atrophy), posterior staphyloma, open-angle glaucoma, early cataract. Myopia tends to give divergent, not convergent, strabismus. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the correct statements:

o.t: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina
Myopia is corrected with convergent lenses
In hyperopia the image forms in front of the retina
Hyperopia is corrected with convergent lenses
Myopia is corrected with divergent lenses

questions.note: Myopia: focus in front of the retina → concave (divergent, minus) lenses. Hyperopia: focus behind the retina → convex (convergent, plus) lenses. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Convergent spherical lenses are used to correct:
questions.note: Plus (convex, convergent) spherical lenses correct hyperopia, presbyopia and aphakia. Myopia → divergent lenses; diplopia → prisms. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical features of heterophoria may include:
questions.note: Heterophoria (latent deviation controlled by fusion): asthenopia – headache, ocular pain/fatigue, blurred vision; the deviation is not visible normally (only on the cover test). A constant or intermittent visible squint = tropia.

questions.q: Paralitical squint has the following features:
questions.note: Paralytic strabismus: diplopia (main symptom), false projection (past-pointing), limited movement and larger deviation in the field of the paralysed muscle, compensatory head posture.

questions.q: Diplopia is a major symptom in
questions.note: Diplopia is the cardinal symptom of PARALYTIC strabismus (acquired); concomitant strabismus in children has suppression/amblyopia, no diplopia.

questions.q: The paralitical strabismus:

o.t: the ocular movement is limited in the direction of the paralised muscle

questions.note: Paralytic strabismus: congenital or acquired, limited movement in the field of the paralysed muscle, VARIABLE deviation angle (larger in that direction, secondary > primary deviation).

questions.q: In the paralytical strabismus the angle deviation is:

o.t: equal in all directions of the gaze
it is higher in the direction of the paralised muscle

questions.note: Paralytic (incomitant) strabismus: the angle increases when looking in the direction of action of the paralysed muscle.

questions.q: An amblyopic eye means that:

o.t: the eye has high intraocular pressure
the eye had a blunt injury

questions.note: Amblyopia ("lazy eye") = decreased best-corrected VA without organic lesion, from abnormal visual experience in childhood.

questions.q: The binocular vision degrees are:
questions.note: Worth's three degrees of binocular vision: simultaneous perception (projection), fusion, stereopsis.

questions.q: In phoria, fusion is:
questions.note: In heterophoria, fusion is present and keeps the eyes aligned; the deviation appears only when fusion is broken (cover test).

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: A diabetic patient presents suddenly with diplopia when looking to the right. Most likely diagnosis is:
questions.note: Diplopia worse looking RIGHT = right lateral rectus (abduction of the right eye) → right VI palsy, the classic microvascular palsy of diabetics.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: In congenital strabismus the functional consequences of the ocular deviation are:
questions.note: Congenital strabismus → amblyopia (low VA of the deviated eye) and loss of binocular vision.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Amblyopia can be observed in the following situations:
questions.note: Amblyopia: deprivation (congenital cataract), anisometropia, strabismus (tropia). Not esophoria, not conjunctivitis.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child has his first ophthalmological consultation. The following investigations are carried out:

o.t: Cover test for the identification of pupillary reflexes
Measuring visual acuity to identify amblyopia
Hirschberg test of corneal reflexes to rule out Claude Bernard Horner’s disease

questions.note: At 3 years: VA (picture charts) for amblyopia, cycloplegic refraction for anisometropia/hyperopia, cover test and Hirschberg (corneal reflexes) for STRABISMUS. Computerised perimetry is not feasible; the cover test is not for pupillary reflexes; Hirschberg is not for Horner.

questions.q: In the case of amblyopia, the following are true:

o.t: Congenital cataracts can be a cause
In case of associated strabismus, it must be corrected before strabismus surgery
Occlusion of the good eye is not indicated
A brain mechanism is responsible for macular neutralization

questions.note: Amblyopia: deprivation (congenital cataract), strabismus, anisometropia; must be treated (occlusion/penalisation of the GOOD eye) BEFORE strabismus surgery; it results from cortical suppression, and binocular vision is affected.

questions.q: Choose the right affirmations for binocular vision:

o.t: The order of the stages of binocular vision is: simultaneous perception, fusion, stereoscopy
Strabismus does not affect binocular vision
Amblyopia is a rare consequence of binocular vision disorder
Congenital nystagmus can be a cause of binocular vision pathology
Binocular vision is possible because the visual field is binocular

questions.note: Worth's degrees: simultaneous perception → fusion → stereopsis. Strabismus disrupts binocular vision; amblyopia is a frequent consequence; congenital nystagmus impairs binocularity. Binocular vision needs overlapping fields of both eyes.

questions.q: In oculomotor nerve (III) palsy:

o.t: The lateral rectus muscle is paralysed

questions.note: Complete III palsy: ptosis, eye "down and out" (divergent, hypotropic, the lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) act unopposed), mydriasis. Pain is present only in compressive (aneurysm) cases, not "frequent" as a feature. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Accommodative strabismus is corrected by:
questions.note: Accommodative esotropia is driven by uncorrected hyperopia (accommodation → convergence); full hyperopic correction with plus (convergent) lenses straightens the eyes. Surgery is not indicated for the purely accommodative form. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In VI (abducens) nerve palsy:

o.t: Adduction of the affected eye is impossible
Abduction of the affected eye is impossible

questions.note: VI palsy → lateral rectus paralysed → esotropia (convergent deviation), limited abduction, horizontal uncrossed diplopia worse in the direction of the paralysed muscle; often microvascular (diabetes) or raised ICP. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Accommodative strabismus:

o.t: Is corrected by wearing convergent lenses
Is corrected by wearing divergent lenses

questions.note: Accommodative esotropia: uncorrected hyperopia → excess accommodation → excess convergence. Treatment: full cycloplegic correction with plus (convergent) lenses; surgery only for a residual non-accommodative component. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In III nerve palsy:

o.t: The direct pupillary reflex is normal
The direct pupillary reflex is abolished
The consensual reflex on stimulating the healthy eye is abolished

questions.note: III palsy = efferent lesion: vision is normal but the affected pupil is dilated and reacts neither directly nor consensually (absolute pupillary rigidity). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In congenital strabismus, the following are true:

o.t: Surgery should be performed in adulthood
The diagnosis also includes the cover test
Amblyopia is seen if the strabismus appears after the age of 7
Convergent strabismus can be associated with hyperopia

questions.note: Strabismus is treated early (glasses → occlusion for amblyopia → surgery in childhood). The cover test is the key diagnostic test. Amblyopia appears when strabismus starts BEFORE ~7 years (sensitive period). Binocular vision is usually lost; esotropia is often accommodative (hyperopia). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Orbital tumours are characterized by:

o.t: Treatment consists of surgery, radiotherapy and/or chemotherapy
Antibiotic therapy should be started without delay

questions.note: Orbital tumours: progressive non-inflammatory exophthalmos (axial for intraconal tumours, displaced/lateral for extraconal), diplopia, optic nerve compression. Treatment: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy according to type. Enophthalmos is seen with scirrhous metastases (breast) but is not the rule.

questions.q: Proptosis or exophthalmos is a typical sign in:
questions.note: Proptosis/exophthalmos is the cardinal sign of orbital disease (thyroid eye disease, tumours, cellulitis).

questions.q: Orbital cellulitis means:

o.t: an inflammation of the orbital osteoperiostum
an inflammation of the fat content of the orbit
an inflammation of the Tenon's capsule
an inflammation of the orbital veins
an inflammation of the orbital segment of the optic nerve

questions.note: Orbital cellulitis = acute infection of the orbital soft tissue / fat behind the septum, usually from ethmoiditis.

questions.q: Orbital miosisis:

o.t: is an infection of the soft tissues behind the orbital septum
is an immunologically induced inflammation which affects an extraocular muscle
there is pain during eye movement

questions.note: Orbital myositis = idiopathic (immune) inflammation of one or more extraocular muscles: pain worse with eye movement, diplopia; treatment = systemic corticosteroids.

questions.q: Causes of inflammatory proptosis are:

o.t: spreading of inflammatory diseases of the eyeball

questions.note: Inflammatory exophthalmos: orbital cellulitis/abscess from sinuses, teeth, eyelids, panophthalmitis, or specific infections (TB, syphilis). Thyroid eye disease is endocrine; trauma is a separate group.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: What is the objective element that differentiates orbital cellulitis from a palpebral abscess (preseptal cellulitis)?

o.t: The existence of a palpebral skin wound
Redness & hot skin around the eyes & eyelids - palpebral (?)

questions.note: Proptosis (with painful/limited eye movement, chemosis, decreased VA) distinguishes post-septal orbital cellulitis from preseptal cellulitis/lid abscess.

questions.q: In orbital cellulitis, the following are true:

o.t: It is an inflammation of the orbital content
Acute dacryocystitis may be the cause
Mydriasis and low visual acuity are possible
Ethmoiditis is a common cause, especially in children

questions.note: Orbital cellulitis = inflammation/infection of orbital content, mainly from ethmoid sinusitis (children); can threaten the optic nerve (decreased VA, RAPD). Acute dacryocystitis gives a preseptal cellulitis more often; retinal haemorrhages are not characteristic.

questions.q: In hyperthyroid disease, possible ocular manifestations are:
questions.note: Thyroid eye disease: dry eye/exposure, conjunctival congestion (over muscle insertions), lid signs (Kocher – staring look, Dalrymple, von Graefe), diplopia from restrictive myopathy, proptosis. Mydriasis is not a feature.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman has known Graves' hyperthyroidism. The following sign may be associated:
questions.note: Thyroid eye disease: upper lid retraction (Dalrymple sign, the most common sign), lid lag (von Graefe), exophthalmos, restrictive myopathy, exposure keratopathy, compressive optic neuropathy. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 23-year-old woman has a red, painful eye with moderate exophthalmos, unchanged visual acuity and fever. The pain increases with eye movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.note: Fever + proptosis + painful/limited eye movements + lid oedema/chemosis (usually from ethmoid sinusitis) = (post-septal) orbital cellulitis – emergency: IV antibiotics, CT. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In congenital dacryocystitis, which sign is most characteristic?

o.t: Reflux of purulent material from the puncta on gentle pressure
Redness of the superior eyelid skin

questions.note: Congenital dacryocystitis: epiphora + mucopurulent reflux from the puncta on pressure over the lacrimal sac (Regurgitation test).

questions.q: Appropriate management for congenital dacryocystitis includes:

o.t: Stab incision if sac is distended with pus

questions.note: Congenital nasolacrimal obstruction / dacryocystitis: lacrimal sac massage (Crigler), warm compresses and topical antibiotics, then probing (catheterism) of the lacrimal pathways. Systemic antibiotics only for acute dacryocystitis with cellulitis; incision is avoided (fistula).

questions.q: The "horizontal S" is a typical sign of:
questions.note: The "horizontal S" (italic S) deformity of the upper eyelid is the classic sign of acute DACRYOADENITIS (enlarged lacrimal gland in the upper-outer lid). Some student keys give "dacryocystitis" – that is wrong: dacryocystitis swells the medial canthus.

questions.q: Dacryoadenitis:

o.t: is the infection of the lacrimal sac
is the inflammation of the lacrimal gland
is secondary to the obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct

questions.note: Dacryoadenitis = inflammation of the lacrimal GLAND (upper-outer lid, S-shaped ptosis). Dacryocystitis = lacrimal sac. Both children and adults.

questions.q: Dacryoadenitis is the inflammation of the:
questions.note: Dacryoadenitis = inflammation of the lacrimal gland.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: The treatment of choice for congenital dacryocystitis consists of:
