questions.note: Probing of the nasolacrimal duct is the treatment of choice in congenital dacryocystitis (after massage + antibiotics).

questions.q: What may be a cause of purulent eye discharge in children?
questions.note: Purulent discharge in a child: dacryocystitis (or bacterial conjunctivitis). Congenital glaucoma: tearing, photophobia, no pus.

questions.q: Three weeks after birth, a child has excessive tearing and mucous discharge. The possible diagnosis is:
questions.note: Epiphora + mucopurulent discharge (reflux from the puncta on pressure) from a few weeks of age = congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction/dacryocystitis. Gonococcal conjunctivitis starts on day 2–4 with hyperpurulent discharge; congenital glaucoma gives tearing + photophobia + big cornea without discharge. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: What is the cause of epiphora?
questions.note: Epiphora = tears overflowing because of impaired DRAINAGE (punctal ectropion, canalicular or nasolacrimal duct obstruction, dacryocystitis). Hypersecretion (lacrimation) is different. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Entropion:

o.t: Is a malposition of the eyelid in which the lid margin is turned towards the globe
Is a malposition of the eyelid in which the lid margin is turned away from the globe
Can be a result of seventh cranial nerve injury
It is a cause of cataract

questions.note: Entropion = lid margin turned towards the globe (lashes rub the cornea); treatment is surgical. VII palsy causes paralytic ECTROPION.

questions.q: Ectropion:

o.t: Is a malposition of the eyelid in which the lid margin is turned towards the globe
Is a malposition of the eyelid in which the lid margin is turned away from the globe
Can be a result of seventh cranial nerve injury

questions.note: Ectropion = lid margin turned away from the globe; forms: involutional, cicatricial, paralytic (VII palsy), mechanical; treatment is surgical. It causes epiphora and exposure, not glaucoma.

questions.q: Which area of the eyelid is typically affected by blepharitis?
questions.note: Blepharitis = chronic inflammation of the LID MARGINS (lashes, follicles, meibomian orifices).

questions.q: Chalazion:

o.t: is an acute infection of the lid glands
may disappear spontaneously or may require surgical treatment

questions.note: Chalazion = chronic lipogranuloma (meibomian cyst), painless nodule; may resolve or need incision–curettage. Acute painful infection = hordeolum.

questions.q: External hordeolum is:

o.t: acute inflammation of lacrimal drainage system.

questions.note: External hordeolum (stye) = acute staphylococcal infection of a Zeis (or Moll) gland at a lash follicle; internal hordeolum = meibomian gland.

questions.q: External sty means:

o.t: an inflammation of the Meibomian gland
an inflammation of the sebaceous gland of the eyelash follicle
an inflammation of the Zeiss gland
an inflammation of the Tenon's capsule

questions.note: External stye = acute suppurative inflammation of the sebaceous glands of Zeis attached to the lash follicle.

questions.q: Ectropion:

o.t: is a malposition of the eyelid in which the lid margin is turned towards the globe
is a malposition of the eyelid in which the lid margin is turned away from the globe
can be paralytical - as a result of seventh cranial nerve injury

questions.note: Ectropion: lid margin turned away from the globe; involutional (elderly), paralytic (VII), cicatricial; treatment is surgical.

questions.q: Spasmodic ectropion is caused by:

o.t: the decreasing skin elasticity due to the age

questions.note: Spastic ectropion is caused by orbicularis spasm in acute conjunctival inflammation (often in children/young with lax skin); involutional ectropion = age-related laxity.

questions.q: Chronic blepharitis can be associated with:

o.t: Seborrheic secretions at the free palpebral margin
Small eyelid ulcers, in the ulcerative form

questions.note: Chronic blepharitis: seborrhoeic scales at the lid margin, staphylococcal form (collarettes, small ulcers in ulcerative blepharitis), meibomian dysfunction. Herpes gives acute vesicular lesions; preseptal cellulitis is not a usual association.

questions.q: The following are true about chalazion:

o.t: It is an infection of the meibomian glands
Chronic blepharitis may be a risk factor for chalazion
Chalazion might need incision, especially massive forms
It is a rare condition of the eyelid

questions.note: Chalazion: chronic sterile lipogranuloma of a meibomian gland (not an infection), no discharge, common; blepharitis/rosacea predispose; large forms need incision–curettage.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man has chronic blepharitis. The following are true:

o.t: Blepharitis may be associated with chalazia
Herpes virus may be the cause
It may be complicated by preseptal cellulitis
The eyelids must be cleaned and seborrhoeic secretions removed

questions.note: Chronic blepharitis (staphylococcal/seborrhoeic, meibomian gland dysfunction) → recurrent chalazia, scales, dry eye; treatment = lid hygiene (warm compresses, cleaning). Herpes gives an acute vesicular blepharitis, not a chronic one; preseptal cellulitis is not a usual complication. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Eyelid entropion:

o.t: Is due to shortness of the skin
Is due to cicatricial retraction of the integument (conjunctiva/tarsus)
Is due to paralysis of the orbicularis muscle

questions.note: Entropion = lid margin turned inward → lashes rub the cornea (trichiasis) → erosions, ulcer. Types: involutional, cicatricial (posterior lamella scarring – trachoma), spastic, congenital. Skin shortness and orbicularis (VII) palsy cause ECTROPION. Single best answer: corneal lesions. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 30-year-old man has recurrent chalazia. The following are true:

o.t: The chalazion can be operated by incision and curettage
Acute herpetic blepharitis may be the cause
Seborrhoeic eyelid secretions may be found
The eyelids must be cleaned and seborrhoeic secretions removed

questions.note: Chalazion = chronic lipogranuloma of a meibomian gland; recurrences are favoured by chronic seborrhoeic/meibomian blepharitis. Treatment: warm compresses, lid hygiene, incision–curettage (biopsy if recurrent at the same site to exclude sebaceous carcinoma). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 36-year-old woman has had episodes of bilateral ocular discomfort with ocular congestion and tearing for 2 years. Symptoms are worse in the morning and the eyelids have crusts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.note: Chronic bilateral irritation worse in the morning + crusts/scales on the lid margins = blepharitis (anterior/staphylococcal or seborrhoeic). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical features of allergic conjunctivitis may include:
questions.note: Allergic conjunctivitis: itching (key symptom), lacrimation/watery discharge, photophobia, chemosis, papillae. Pain on eye movement = orbital or optic nerve inflammation; scleral necrosis = necrotising scleritis.

questions.q: Which medication is used in allergic conjunctivitis?
questions.note: Of these options only systemic steroids (oral prednisone) treat a severe allergic reaction; the usual treatment is topical antihistamines/mast-cell stabilisers (olopatadine, ketotifen), cold compresses, short courses of topical steroids. Antibiotics/antivirals/glaucoma drugs have no role.

questions.q: The following statements are FALSE about acute conjunctivitis:

o.t: Is a contagious disease fostered by crowded conditions
Differential diagnosis with acute keratitis, acute uveitis, acute glaucoma

questions.note: FALSE statements: the eye must NOT be bandaged in conjunctivitis (incubator for bacteria) and the eye is RED, not white. Correct: contagious, DDx with keratitis/uveitis/acute glaucoma, discomfort and foreign-body sensation.

questions.q: Signs and symptoms in acute catarrhal conjunctivitis:

o.t: red eye - superficial congestion of the conjunctiva
the patient complains of foreign-body sensation

questions.note: Catarrhal (viral/allergic) conjunctivitis: superficial diffuse congestion, watery/mucous discharge, foreign-body sensation, often bilateral. Purulent discharge = bacterial.

questions.q: Signs and symptoms in acute catarrhal conjunctivitis:

o.t: oedema and superficial congestion of the conjunctiva

questions.note: Catarrhal conjunctivitis: oedema + superficial congestion, tearing, chemosis; not purulent.

questions.q: Pseudomembranous conjunctivitis is caused by:
questions.note: Pseudomembranous/membranous conjunctivitis: classically Corynebacterium diphtheriae (true membranes), also adenovirus, streptococcus, gonococcus.

questions.q: Gonococcal conjunctivitis appears after birth in:
questions.note: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum begins 2–4 (up to 5) days after birth; chlamydial at 5–14 days.

questions.q: Prophylaxy in gonococcal conjunctivitis is made by:

o.t: instillation of 1 drop of AgNO3 just immediately after birth
instillation of 1 drop of Penicillin just immediately after birth

questions.note: Classic Credé prophylaxis = 1 % silver nitrate drop immediately after birth (today erythromycin/tetracycline ointment or povidone-iodine).

questions.q: In adenoviral conjunctivitis, the following can be observed:

o.t: The duration of conjunctivitis is greatly reduced if antibiotic treatment is promptly initiated.

questions.note: Adenoviral conjunctivitis (epidemic keratoconjunctivitis / pharyngoconjunctival fever): follicles, watery discharge, tender pre-auricular node, fever, pharyngitis, rhinitis; self-limiting – antibiotics do not shorten it. Giant papillae = allergic/contact lens.

questions.q: The following statements are true about acute conjunctivitis:

o.t: Contagious viral diseases are common causes
Eye dressing helps with the pain caused by blinking
Secretions should be washed off with water
The systemic antibiotic is indicated in case of conjunctivitis of the newborn

questions.note: Acute conjunctivitis: commonly viral and contagious; wash secretions; systemic antibiotics for neonatal (gonococcal/chlamydial) conjunctivitis; NEVER patch; not every red eye is conjunctivitis.

questions.q: In cobblestone (giant papillary / vernal) conjunctivitis you may observe:

o.t: A contact lens worn longer than normal
Pre-auricular lymphadenopathy, if the aetiology is viral

questions.note: Cobblestone = giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva (vernal keratoconjunctivitis or giant papillary conjunctivitis from contact-lens overwear) with stringy mucous discharge. Follicles and pre-auricular nodes belong to viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis, not to cobblestones. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In front of a red eye, which signs support the diagnosis of conjunctivitis?
questions.note: Conjunctivitis: diffuse superficial (peripheral) hyperaemia, discharge, foreign-body/sand sensation, normal VA and normal IOP. Decreased VA or high IOP point to keratitis, uveitis or acute glaucoma. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Two patients present to the emergency room. Patient 1: conjunctival congestion, pain, loss of vision. Patient 2: conjunctival congestion, burning, foreign-body sensation. Only patient 1 is kept in hospital. Why?

o.t: Patient 1 is diagnosed with acute conjunctivitis
Patient 2 has an ocular foreign body which must not be removed
Patient 2 has acute conjunctivitis which can be treated at home
Patient 1 has more pain than patient 2

questions.note: A red painful eye WITH decreased vision is an emergency (keratitis, uveitis, acute glaucoma). Red eye with burning/grittiness and normal vision = conjunctivitis, treated as outpatient. A superficial foreign body is always removed. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 26-year-old man has had episodes of bilateral ocular discomfort with itching, conjunctival congestion and oedema for 2 years. Symptoms are worse in spring and hypertrophic papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.note: Itching + seasonal (spring) recurrence + giant/hypertrophic tarsal papillae = allergic (vernal/seasonal) conjunctivitis; treatment: antihistamines/mast-cell stabilisers, short steroid courses. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the red-eye situations with peripheral (superficial) conjunctival congestion:
questions.note: Superficial (conjunctival) hyperaemia, maximal in the fornices and fading towards the limbus = conjunctivitis. Iridocyclitis, keratitis and acute glaucoma give deep perikeratic (ciliary) injection; scleritis gives deep violaceous injection. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient has a red, painless eye, unchanged visual acuity and abundant clear (watery) conjunctival discharge. What is the cause?
questions.note: Watery discharge + normal VA + no pain (often follicles, pre-auricular node, recent URTI, bilateralisation) = viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis. Bacterial gives mucopurulent discharge. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Clinical features of Herpes Simplex epithelial keratitis include:

o.t: Dendritic branching ulcer staining with fluorescein

questions.note: HSV epithelial keratitis: dendritic ulcer whose bed stains with fluorescein, DECREASED corneal sensitivity, watery discharge, often miosis (reflex). Coarse punctate lesions are rather adenoviral/zoster.

questions.q: What treatment is contraindicated in active epithelial herpetic keratitis?
questions.note: Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated in active epithelial HSV keratitis (they enhance viral replication → geographic ulcer, perforation). Antivirals, debridement and a bandage lens are acceptable.

questions.q: Risk factors for Zona Zoster Ophthalmicus include:
questions.note: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1): reactivation favoured by old age, HIV/AIDS, diabetes, cancer, immunosuppressive therapy. III palsy is a possible COMPLICATION, not a risk factor.

questions.q: Risk factors for microbial (exogenous) keratitis include:
questions.note: Microbial keratitis risk factors: contact lenses (most important; swimming/water exposure with lenses → Acanthamoeba), ocular surface disease (dry eye, exposure, trichiasis), chronic dacryocystitis (bacterial reservoir), immunosuppression (local/systemic steroids, diabetes).

questions.q: A 35-years old patient has a moderate loss of visual acuity associated with ocular discomfort and photophobia. The fluorescein coloration demonstrates a dendritic corneal lesion. The diagnosis is:
questions.note: Dendritic fluorescein-positive lesion = superficial (epithelial) herpetic keratitis.

questions.q: the corneal ulcer is characterized by :
questions.note: Corneal ulcer: epithelial and stromal loss (ulceration, fluorescein +), often after trauma; may have hypopyon (sterile pus in the AC) and reflex miosis. (Miosis is also accepted by many corrections.)

questions.q: The treatment of herpes simplex keratitis consists of:
questions.note: HSV keratitis: topical antivirals (aciclovir) ± cycloplegic (atropine) for comfort/ciliary spasm; steroids are contraindicated in the epithelial form; pilocarpine has no role.

questions.q: The treatment of herpes simplex keratitis with active epithelial disease consists of:
questions.note: Active epithelial HSV disease: topical antiviral (aciclovir ointment / ganciclovir gel), debridement; no steroids.

questions.q: The treatment of herpes simplex keratitis consists of:
questions.note: HSV keratitis: antivirals (topical, oral for stromal/recurrent forms) + cycloplegics (atropine) when there is uveal reaction.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Bacterial corneal ulcer presents the following features:
questions.note: Bacterial ulcer: central/paracentral greyish-white infiltrate with epithelial defect, mucopurulent discharge, often after trauma/contact lens; dendritic = HSV; intact epithelium = stromal keratitis.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Complications of herpetic keratitis are: (dafuq?)

o.t: Excruciating pain in the dermatomeric region of eruption

questions.note: HSV keratitis complications: stromal keratitis/scarring (leucoma), superinfection, thinning and perforation, neurotrophic ulcer, uveitis/glaucoma. Dermatomal pain = zoster; leukocoria is unrelated.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: When treating superficial herpetic keratitis all the preparations below are indicated, EXCEPT:
questions.note: EXCEPT: corticosteroids are contraindicated in superficial (epithelial) HSV keratitis. Aciclovir, cycloplegics and prophylactic antibiotic drops are acceptable.

questions.q: In lagophthalmic keratitis, the following are possible:
questions.note: Lagophthalmos = incomplete lid closure: facial palsy, severe exophthalmos (Graves), ectropion, scarring → exposure → dry inferior cornea → punctate erosions/ulcer. Trigeminal (V) palsy gives NEUROTROPHIC keratitis, not lagophthalmic. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient has a central corneal ulcer 3 days after ocular trauma with a fir-tree branch. The following are true:

o.t: Herpes simplex is the cause in this case
Purulent secretions in the ulcer are frequent

questions.note: Vegetal trauma → infectious keratitis (bacterial; fungal must be suspected with plant matter): fluorescein-positive ulcer with a purulent infiltrate, ± hypopyon. Herpes is reactivation, not trauma-related; treatment = intensive broad-spectrum (± antifungal) drops after scraping for culture. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient has a moderate decrease of visual acuity in the left eye with moderate pain. Examination: perikeratic (ciliary) conjunctival congestion, positive fluorescein staining with a dendritic shape. What is the diagnosis?
questions.note: A dendritic fluorescein-positive ulcer = HSV epithelial (superficial) keratitis; treated with topical antivirals (aciclovir/ganciclovir), NO steroids. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient has a moderate decrease in visual acuity with ocular discomfort and photophobia. Fluorescein staining shows a dendritic corneal lesion. What is the diagnosis?
questions.note: Dendritic ulcer = HSV epithelial (superficial) keratitis. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.exam: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: The following could be causes of lagophthalmic keratopathy, EXCEPT one:
questions.note: Lagophthalmos (incomplete closure) → exposure keratopathy: facial palsy, severe exophthalmos (Graves), ectropion, lid scarring. Entropion damages the cornea by trichiasis, not by exposure.

questions.q: In acute iritis, the following are observed:
questions.note: Acute iritis: ciliary (red) eye, miosis, irregular pupil from posterior synechiae, keratic precipitates, flare/cells, endothelial oedema. No purulent discharge.

questions.q: Signs of iritis are:

o.t: congestion of the conjunctiva in the perilimbal region

questions.note: Iritis: perilimbal (ciliary) congestion, endothelial oedema/keratic precipitates, miosis; the iris is swollen with blurred pattern (muddy, not grey). Vitreous exudates = cyclitis/posterior.

questions.q: The typical signs of pure cyclitis are:

o.t: congestion of the conjunctiva around the limbus

questions.note: Pure cyclitis (intermediate uveitis): white or slightly injected eye, retrolental and vitreous exudates/opacities ("snowballs"), fluctuating IOP (ciliary body secretion disturbed). Keratic precipitates, miosis and hypopyon are typical of iritis.

questions.q: Complications of cyclitis:
questions.note: Chronic cyclitis: complicated cataract, secondary glaucoma (or hypotony), macular oedema, ciliary body failure → atrophia/phthisis bulbi.

questions.q: Toxic exogenes iridocyclitis is caused by:
questions.note: Toxic exogenous iridocyclitis = from chemical burns of the cornea/sclera (toxins penetrate). Penetrating wounds give infectious (or sympathetic) uveitis.

questions.q: A red, congestive eye with low visual acuity has a miotic pupil. The most likely cause is the following:
questions.note: Red eye + low VA + miosis = iridocyclitis. Acute glaucoma gives a mid-dilated pupil; Horner gives miosis in a WHITE eye.

questions.q: In ocular toxoplasmosis, the following statements are true:

o.t: Contamination with infected secretions is the pathogenic mechanism
Granuloma of the ciliary body is the characteristic lesion
The congenital form may lead to bilateral low vision

questions.note: Ocular toxoplasmosis: necrotising retinochoroiditis, often MACULAR (congenital macular scars → bilateral low vision), transmitted transplacentally or by ingestion (cysts/oocysts), white eye usually.

questions.q: Causes of endophthalmitis can be:
questions.note: Exogenous endophthalmitis: post-operative (cataract surgery), post-traumatic (penetrating wound, retained foreign body), perforated corneal ulcer; endogenous: septicaemia / bacteraemia. Retinal detachment is not infectious. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the possible causes of uveitis:
questions.note: Uveitis: autoimmune/rheumatic diseases (ankylosing spondylitis, JIA, RA – mainly scleritis but also uveitis), infections (Lyme, toxoplasma, herpes, TB, syphilis) and focal infections (dental/ENT foci). Hypoparathyroidism gives cataract; atherosclerosis gives vascular occlusions. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Manifestations of anterior uveitis are:
questions.note: Anterior uveitis: ciliary (perilimbal) injection, miosis, keratic precipitates, aqueous flare and cells, hypopyon, posterior synechiae, IOP changes. Retinal detachment is not an anterior uveitis sign. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Toxoplasmic chorioretinitis in adults presents the following signs and symptoms:

o.t: A white, fluffy (blurred) focus at the fundus (macular granuloma)

questions.note: Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis: a white fluffy active focus often next to a pigmented scar ("headlight in the fog" with vitritis), floaters and decreased VA when macular. It is a posterior uveitis: usually white eye, no synechiae, no neovessels. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Complications of anterior uveitis are:
questions.note: Anterior uveitis → posterior synechiae (seclusio/occlusio pupillae), complicated cataract, secondary glaucoma (inflammatory, angle closure by synechiae), band keratopathy, macular oedema. RD and orbital cellulitis are not typical. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Regarding uveitis, which statements are correct?

o.t: The eye is red and painful
It may be complicated by glaucoma
It may be treated with miotic eye drops
It may be treated with corticosteroid eye drops

questions.note: Anterior uveitis: painful red eye, photophobia, decreased vision; complications: glaucoma, cataract, synechiae. Treatment: topical corticosteroids + mydriatics/cycloplegics (NEVER miotics, which favour posterior synechiae). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient has a unilateral decrease in vision in a red, painful eye. Choose the possible diagnoses:
questions.note: Red painful eye with decreased VA: keratitis, acute anterior uveitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, endophthalmitis, scleritis. Conjunctivitis does not reduce VA; vascular occlusions are painless with a white eye. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient has a moderate decrease in visual acuity with ocular discomfort and photophobia. The pupil is miotic and the cornea is clear. What is the diagnosis?
questions.note: Photophobia + decreased VA + miosis + clear cornea (no fluorescein staining) = anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis): ciliary injection, keratic precipitates, flare. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient has a moderate decrease in visual acuity of the left eye with moderate pain. Examination: perikeratic conjunctival congestion, clear cornea and a miotic pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.note: Ciliary injection + clear cornea + miosis = acute iritis (anterior uveitis). Keratitis has a corneal lesion; acute glaucoma has a mid-dilated pupil and corneal oedema. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Select the situations in which visual acuity drops suddenly in a red, painful eye:
questions.note: Red painful eye with decreased VA: keratitis, anterior uveitis, acute glaucoma. Conjunctivitis keeps normal VA; cataract is progressive; CRAO is painless with a white eye. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the red-eye situations with pupillary changes:
questions.note: Iridocyclitis → miosis (± irregular pupil from synechiae); acute angle closure → fixed mid-dilated pupil. Conjunctivitis, scleritis and subconjunctival haemorrhage leave the pupil normal. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The typical signs of pure iritis are:

o.t: Congestion of the conjunctiva around the limbus

questions.note: Pure iritis (anterior uveitis): perilimbal (ciliary) congestion, keratic precipitates, miosis, aqueous flare/cells, hypopyon in severe cases. Vitreous/retrolental exudates and IOP fluctuation belong to cyclitis.

questions.q: Causes of pathological cataract include:
questions.note: Pathological (secondary/complicated) cataract: diabetes, corticosteroids, hypocalcaemia, uveitis, myotonic dystrophy, atopic dermatitis, radiation. Hypertension, RA and migraine are not classic causes.

questions.q: Signs of subluxated lens are:

o.t: anterior chamber is of unequal depth
the lens is in the anterior chamber
the lens is in the vitreous

questions.note: Lens subluxation: unequal anterior chamber depth, iridodonesis/phacodonesis, vitreous in the anterior chamber, the lens edge visible in the pupil. Lens in AC or vitreous = complete luxation.

questions.q: Signs of subluxated lens are:
questions.note: Subluxated lens: unequal anterior chamber depth, iridodonesis, irido-phacodonesis, vitreous prolapse into the AC.

questions.q: Zonular cataract is

o.t: The opacity localized perinuclear, but the nucleus and lens periphery remain clear
The opacification of the whole lens

questions.note: Zonular (lamellar) cataract: congenital opacity of a perinuclear zone (lamella) with clear nucleus and periphery – the most common congenital cataract.

questions.q: Secondary cataract appears after:

o.t: incomplete resorption of the direct traumatic cataract

questions.note: "Secondary cataract" = posterior capsule opacification after extracapsular extraction (Elschnig pearls) or after incomplete resorption of a traumatic cataract; treated with YAG capsulotomy. (Complicated cataract = cataract due to uveitis, etc.)

questions.q: Complicated cataract appears in:
questions.note: Complicated/pathological cataract: endocrine (diabetes, hypoparathyroidism), chronic uveitis, skin diseases (atopic dermatitis), retinitis pigmentosa, myotonic dystrophy.

questions.q: complicated cataract apperas in:
questions.note: Complicated cataract: glaucoma (and its surgery), diabetes, hypocalcaemia, Wilson (sunflower cataract), steroids, chronic uveitis, retinitis pigmentosa, intraocular tumours. Hypothyroidism is not a classic cause (hypoPARAthyroidism is).

questions.q: Pathological cataract appears in:
questions.note: Pathological cataract: recurrent uveitis, endocrine diseases, myotonic dystrophy, retinal detachment (long-standing), glaucoma (acute attack, surgery), skin diseases.

questions.q: A 68-years old patient presents with bilateral progressive loss of visual acuity, more pronounced in the right eye. Which are the possible causes?
questions.note: Bilateral, progressive, asymmetric loss in an elderly patient: cataract and AMD (also glaucoma, diabetic maculopathy). CRVO and ischaemic optic neuropathy are sudden.

questions.q: A 67-year-old patient presents with slow decline in visual acuity in the left eye over 2 years. Possible diagnosis:
questions.note: Slow decline over 2 years in an elderly patient: cataract or (dry) AMD.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: In cataract surgery the most frequent complications are:

o.t: EndophthalmitisD) Ocular hemorrhage E) Retinal detachment

questions.note: Cataract surgery complications: posterior capsule rupture, endophthalmitis, haemorrhage (expulsive/suprachoroidal), retinal detachment, cystoid macular oedema, posterior capsule opacification.

questions.q: In advanced cataracts we can observe the following complications:
questions.note: Advanced cataract: phacomorphic (intumescent) and phacolytic (hypermature) secondary glaucoma, phaco-anaphylactic uveitis, lens subluxation.

questions.q: The following diseases may be complicated by cataract:
questions.note: Complicated (secondary) cataract: chronic uveitis/iridocyclitis, high myopia, acute angle-closure (glaukomflecken), retinitis pigmentosa, retinal detachment. Conjunctivitis and astigmatism do not cause cataract. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the causes of progressive visual loss from the following list:
questions.note: Cataract and AMD progress slowly; CRAO and AION are sudden; acute keratitis is acute with a painful red eye. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the possible complications during the evolution of a cataract:
questions.note: Untreated cataract: intumescent (phacomorphic) angle-closure glaucoma, hypermature cataract → phacolytic glaucoma, phaco-anaphylactic uveitis, lens subluxation/luxation (Morgagnian cataract, weak zonules). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 66-year-old man reports gradual bilateral loss of vision, more marked on the right. Possible diagnoses are:
questions.note: Gradual bilateral asymmetric loss in the elderly: cataract, AMD, glaucoma, diabetic maculopathy. Vein occlusion and AION are sudden and usually unilateral. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Methods for measuring the intraocular pressure are:
questions.note: IOP is measured by tonometry: Goldmann applanation (gold standard), non-contact air-puff, Schiøtz indentation, rebound. Refractometry = refraction, perimetry = visual field, keratometry = corneal curvature. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Normal intraocular pressure:

o.t: Is measured after a penetrating corneal wound
Can be measured by applanation tonometry (Goldmann)
Is present in all congenital glaucomas

questions.note: Normal IOP ≈ 10–21 mmHg, measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry. Tonometry is contraindicated with an open globe; IOP is high in acute and congenital glaucoma. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Glaucoma:

o.t: Is the opacification of the lens
Is associated with high intraocular pressure
Does not affect the optic nerve

questions.note: Glaucoma = progressive optic neuropathy, usually with raised IOP, producing characteristic visual field defects; it also exists in children (congenital glaucoma). Lens opacification = cataract.

questions.q: Neovascular glaucoma may be present in the following conditions:
questions.note: Neovascular glaucoma follows retinal/ocular ischaemia: proliferative diabetic retinopathy, ischaemic CRVO, ocular ischaemic syndrome; also chronic uveitis. Keratitis and cataract are not causes.

questions.q: In acute glaucoma, the following are observed:
questions.note: Acute angle closure: IOP 40–80 mmHg, vertically oval mid-dilated fixed pupil, shallow anterior chamber, corneal oedema, red eye.

questions.q: Signs in acute angle-closure glaucoma:
questions.note: Acute angle-closure glaucoma: red eye, corneal oedema, fixed mid-dilated pupil, very high IOP.

questions.q: Signs in angle-closure glaucoma are:
questions.note: Angle closure: red eye, corneal oedema (hazy cornea), fixed mid-dilated pupil, elevated IOP. Not a white eye, no corneal ulcer, IOP not normal.

questions.q: Signs in acute glaucoma are:
questions.note: Acute glaucoma: conjunctival (ciliary) congestion, IOP ≈ 50 mmHg, mydriasis (fixed mid-dilated pupil), shallow anterior chamber.

questions.q: In angle closure glaucoma the surgical treatment is:

o.t: is not mandatory if the IOP decreases with topical anti-glaucomatous drugs.

questions.note: Angle-closure glaucoma: after medical lowering of IOP, laser (or surgical) peripheral iridotomy is mandatory in both eyes; medical treatment alone is not definitive.

questions.q: Surgery is indicates in open angular glaucoma:

o.t: If the IOP decreases under 22 mmHg
If the IOP decreases under 22 mmHg but the visual function decreases as well
If the IOP does not decrease under 20 mmHg
If the eye is hyperopic no matter of the IOP values

questions.note: POAG surgery (trabeculectomy) when target IOP is not reached with maximal tolerated treatment, or when the field/disc keeps deteriorating despite "normal" IOP.

questions.q: Causes of secondary glaucoma:
questions.note: Secondary glaucoma: intumescent (phacomorphic) and hypermature (phacolytic) cataract, pupillary block (seclusio pupillae, pupillary membrane), neovascular (diabetic retinopathy, CRVO), uveitis, trauma, steroids. (Diabetic retinopathy → neovascular glaucoma is also correct.)

questions.q: Causes of secondary glaucoma:
questions.note: Secondary glaucoma: intumescent cataract, neovascular glaucoma (diabetic retinopathy, CRVO), uveitis. Conjunctivitis is not a cause.

questions.q: Neovascular glaucoma is a complication of:
questions.note: Neovascular glaucoma: diabetic retinopathy, CRVO (ischaemic), CRAO (less often), severe hypertensive/ocular ischaemic retinopathy – any chronic retinal ischaemia.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Choose the true statements about primary open-angle glaucoma:

o.t: Poor visual acuity is typical for the early onset

questions.note: POAG: chronic progressive optic neuropathy with raised IOP (risk factor), can lead to blindness, needs lifelong follow-up; VF is affected (arcuate defects) while central VA stays good until late stages.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: The following signs characterize acute primary angle-closure glaucoma:
questions.note: Acute angle closure: shallow (narrow) anterior chamber, severe pain, conjunctival/ciliary congestion, mid-dilated fixed pupil (NOT miosis), no purulent discharge.

questions.q: A patient presents with red eye, intense pain, and decreased vision. The following diagnoses are NOT likely:
questions.note: Red, painful eye with decreased vision = acute glaucoma, keratitis, uveitis. NOT likely: CRVO (painless white eye), purulent conjunctivitis (normal vision), neovascular AMD (painless), cataract (painless).

questions.q: No light perception can be observed in the following uncomplicated disease:
questions.note: No light perception: end-stage (absolute) glaucoma. Uncomplicated cataract always keeps light perception (with good projection); AMD keeps peripheral vision; iridocyclitis does not abolish light perception.

questions.q: In acute glaucoma, the following are observed:
questions.note: Acute glaucoma: IOP 40–80 mmHg, mid-dilated pupil, corneal oedema, hemicranial headache, nausea/vomiting.

questions.q: Neovascular glaucoma may be present in the following conditions:

o.t: Obstruction of the central retinal vein

questions.note: Neovascular glaucoma: proliferative DR, CRVO (ischaemic).

questions.q: A patient with diabetes known for 12 years presents with decreased vision, ocular pain and marked redness of one eye. Which of the following causes is most likely?
questions.note: Retinal ischaemia (proliferative diabetic retinopathy) → VEGF → iris and angle neovessels → painful red eye with high IOP. Vitreous haemorrhage and retinal detachment are painless with a white eye. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which eye diseases can be complicated by neovascular glaucoma?
questions.note: Neovascular glaucoma follows retinal ischaemia: proliferative diabetic retinopathy, ischaemic CRVO ("100-day glaucoma"), ocular ischaemic syndrome, CRAO. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the signs and symptoms specific to primary open-angle glaucoma:

o.t: Enlargement of the optic disc cup

questions.note: POAG is painless; the disc shows an enlarged (vertical) cup with neuroretinal rim thinning; VF: paracentral and arcuate (Bjerrum) scotomas, nasal step; central vision is spared until the end. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 65-year-old patient has a sudden unilateral loss of vision in a red and very painful eye, with headache, nausea and vomiting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.note: Acute angle-closure glaucoma: severe pain, halos, headache, nausea/vomiting, red eye, corneal oedema, fixed mid-dilated pupil, shallow anterior chamber, IOP 50–70 mmHg, rock-hard eye. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the changes in primary open-angle glaucoma:

o.t: Enlargement of the optic disc cup

questions.note: POAG: raised IOP (main risk factor, though normal-tension forms exist), progressive cupping with rim loss, arcuate/paracentral field defects. Disc swelling with blurred margins suggests papilloedema/AION; central scotoma is late. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: What is the cause of buphthalmos?
questions.note: Buphthalmos ("ox eye") = enlargement of the globe and cornea in primary congenital glaucoma because the infant's sclera/cornea stretch under raised IOP. Triad: epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A patient with proliferative diabetic retinopathy may present with the following characteristics, EXCEPT one:

o.t: Neovascularization involving the optic disk, retina or iris

questions.note: PDR: neovessels (disc/retina/iris), vitreous haemorrhage, TRACTIONAL retinal detachment, plus background lesions (dot-blot haemorrhages). Exudative RD is not a feature of PDR.

questions.q: Choroidal melanoma:

o.t: It is an elevated subretinal brown lesion

questions.note: Choroidal melanoma = the most frequent primary malignant intraocular tumour in adults, unilateral, elevated brown (sometimes amelanotic) subretinal mass, often with secondary exudative retinal detachment.

questions.q: Retinoblastoma:

o.t: The onset can be with strabismus

questions.note: Retinoblastoma: malignant retinal tumour of young children (mostly < 3 y), presenting with leukocoria (1st) and strabismus (2nd); white tumour on fundus.

questions.q: in retinal vein occlusion appears :

o.t: areteries are very thin ,often appear obliterated

questions.note: Retinal vein occlusion: diffuse flame haemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins, retinal/macular oedema, cotton-wool spots. Thin arteries and cherry-red spot = artery occlusion.

questions.q: Background diabetic retinopathy is characterized by:
questions.note: Background (non-proliferative) DR: microaneurysms, dot-and-blot (intraretinal) haemorrhages, hard exudates. Cotton-wool spots and flame haemorrhages point to pre-proliferative/hypertensive changes.

questions.q: In nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy the fundus reveals:
questions.note: NPDR: microaneurysms, haemorrhages and exudates, macular oedema; fibrovascular tissue and neovessels = proliferative.

questions.q: Pigmentary retinopathy is caused because of a deficit of:
questions.note: Retinitis pigmentosa = inherited rod–cone dystrophy: rods are affected first → night blindness and peripheral field loss.

questions.q: Retinoblastoma appears:

o.t: at children after 8 years of age

questions.note: Retinoblastoma: young children, mostly 1–3 years (90 % before 5 y).

questions.q: The most frequent clinical presentation of retinoblastoma is:
questions.note: Leukocoria is the most frequent presenting sign; strabismus is the second.

questions.q: Choroidal malignant melanoma:

o.t: is the most frequently occurring intraocular tumor in adults
surgery is never a treatment option
may produce retinal detachment as a complication

questions.note: Choroidal melanoma: most frequent primary intraocular malignancy in adults, can be asymptomatic (found on routine fundus), causes exudative RD; treatment: brachytherapy/proton beam or enucleation. Unilateral.

questions.q: Secondary retinal detachment appears after:
questions.note: Secondary (non-rhegmatogenous) RD: tractional (penetrating injury, PDR), exudative (choroiditis, choroidal tumours, Harada, toxaemia).

questions.q: In central retinal artery occlusion at the examination of the fundus we find:

o.t: "Cherry red spot" aspect of the macula

questions.note: CRAO fundus: milky-white retinal oedema, thin (narrow) arteries with segmented flow, cherry-red spot.

questions.q: The modifications of the fundus in pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy:
questions.note: Pre-proliferative (severe NPDR): microaneurysms, many haemorrhages (dot and large blot), hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities), venous beading. New vessels = proliferative.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: The following statements are correct for age-related macular degeneration

o.t: It is a very rare condition
The main functional loss is the peripheral visual field
If taken proper care of early, ophthalmological treatment is able to cure the disease
Drusen are seen early in the disease
Intraocular injection can be used for the neovascular form

questions.note: AMD: frequent (leading cause of blindness in the elderly), affects CENTRAL vision, drusen are the early sign, wet form treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF (no cure).

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: In a patient with decompensated diabetes (VA 2/50), possible causes of decreased vision include:
questions.note: Decreased VA in a diabetic: cataract, macular oedema, vitreous haemorrhage from PDR, tractional RD, neovascular glaucoma. RRD is not a specific diabetic complication.

questions.q: The obstruction of the central retinal artery may present with the following characteristics:
questions.note: CRAO: retinal pallor (whitening) with cherry-red spot, thin arteries; poor prognosis; no massive haemorrhages (= CRVO), no cupping (= glaucoma).

questions.q: Retinoblastoma:

o.t: It can manifest clinically with leukocoria
It can manifest clinically with strabismus
It is a whitish tumor *11. The following could represent causes for lagophthalmos keratopathy, except one: A. Basedow disease B. Ectropion C. Entropion D. Facial nerve paralysis

questions.note: Retinoblastoma: malignant, children, white tumour presenting with leukocoria or strabismus.

questions.q: In central venous occlusions there are:
questions.note: CRVO: retinal oedema, dilated tortuous veins, haemorrhages in all quadrants, cotton-wool spots; quiet eye. Cherry-red spot = CRAO.

questions.q: In age-related macular degeneration, the following are true:

o.t: The peripheral visual field is the first to be affected

questions.note: AMD: multifactorial (age, genetics, smoking – the main modifiable risk factor); central vision is affected first; no curative surgery; anti-VEGF for wet AMD; AREDS supplementation slows progression.

questions.q: Lesions in diabetic retinopathy, proliferative stage can be:
questions.note: PDR: neovessels (disc/elsewhere) plus all background lesions (haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, IRMA); vitreous haemorrhage, tractional RD. Disc cupping = glaucoma.

questions.q: The following are valid for the macula:

o.t: In the macula there are mostly Rod-type photoreceptor cells
The image is formed in front of the macula if the eye is hypermetropic
It is found in the nasal area of the retina
It is responsible for visual acuity

questions.note: Macula: cone-rich centre, responsible for VA, examined by ophthalmoscopy/OCT, located temporal to the disc. In hyperopia the image forms BEHIND the retina.

questions.q: Which of the following conditions can cause immediate total blindness?
questions.note: CRAO: sudden, painless, near-total loss of vision (counting fingers / light perception) within seconds. RD progresses over hours/days, a branch vein occlusion affects only a sector, cataract is progressive. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: At fundus examination, a brown raised retinal lesion is seen in a 65-year-old patient. The following are true:

o.t: Ocular ultrasound can help in the differential diagnosis
A possible diagnosis is choroidal melanoma. If confirmed, the eye must be enucleated
A possible diagnosis is choroidal naevus. If confirmed, metastases must be searched for

questions.note: A pigmented elevated choroidal lesion in an adult = naevus vs melanoma; ultrasound (low internal reflectivity, height, choroidal excavation) and angiography help. Retinoblastoma is a white tumour of young children. Melanoma is not always enucleated (brachytherapy/proton therapy for small–medium tumours). A naevus is benign (no metastatic work-up). Biopsy is rarely needed. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In central retinal artery occlusion one may observe:
questions.note: CRAO: diffuse retinal whitening (ischaemic oedema) with a cherry-red spot at the fovea, thin arteries, "box-car" segmentation, sometimes a visible embolus (cholesterol/Hollenhorst plaque). Numerous haemorrhages and tortuous veins are CRVO. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Fundus examination in diabetic retinopathy can show:
questions.note: DR: microaneurysms (first sign), dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, neovessels (proliferative). The detachment of PDR is TRACTIONAL, not rhegmatogenous. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: At fundus examination, a brown raised retinal lesion is seen in a 65-year-old patient. The following are true:

o.t: Ocular ultrasound can help in the differential diagnosis of tumours
If choroidal melanoma is confirmed, the eye must be enucleated
A rhegmatogenous retinal detachment is likely

questions.note: Ultrasound (A/B-scan) is the key test for choroidal tumours. Retinoblastoma = children, white mass. Enucleation is reserved for large melanomas; smaller ones receive brachytherapy. A melanoma may give an exudative (not rhegmatogenous) detachment. Biopsy is not routine. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: What is the condition required for a (rhegmatogenous) retinal detachment to occur?

o.t: Dense nuclear cataract with a clear cortex

questions.note: Rhegmatogenous RD requires a retinal break (tear/hole) + liquefied vitreous passing through it under the neurosensory retina. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the causes of progressive loss of vision:
questions.note: Progressive: cataract, AMD (dry), diabetic maculopathy, glaucoma, refractive errors. CRAO and AION are sudden. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Select the situations in which visual acuity drops suddenly in a white, painless eye:
questions.note: Sudden painless loss in a white eye: CRAO, CRVO, AION, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, wet AMD. Keratitis and uveitis give a red painful eye; cataract is progressive. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 3-month-old baby is brought by the mother for leukocoria. Possible diagnoses are:
questions.note: Leukocoria (white pupil): congenital cataract, retinoblastoma (must be excluded first), persistent fetal vasculature, ROP, Coats disease, coloboma, toxocara. Congenital glaucoma gives a large hazy cornea, not leukocoria. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 76-year-old man reports a sudden unilateral decrease in vision in a quiet, painless eye. Possible diagnoses are:
questions.note: Sudden painless loss in a white eye in an elderly patient: AION (rule out giant cell arteritis), CRAO, CRVO, vitreous haemorrhage, wet AMD, RD. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In central retinal vein occlusion:

o.t: The amplitude of the direct pupillary light reflex is decreased
The optic disc margin is blurred

questions.note: CRVO: "blood and thunder" fundus – flame haemorrhages in all quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, cotton-wool spots, disc and macular oedema (blurred disc); RAPD in the ischaemic form. Pale retina = CRAO. Painless (unless neovascular glaucoma). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the risk factors for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment:
questions.note: RRD risk factors: high myopia, lattice degeneration, posterior vitreous detachment, cataract surgery (pseudophakia/aphakia, especially with posterior capsule rupture), trauma, previous RD in the fellow eye. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Laser photocoagulation of the retina is indicated in:
questions.note: Panretinal photocoagulation destroys ischaemic retina to stop VEGF production: proliferative DR (and severe NPDR), ischaemic vein occlusion with neovessels. Angle closure is treated by laser IRIDOTOMY (not retinal photocoagulation); atrophic AMD has no laser treatment. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the correct statements about AMD:

o.t: Metamorphopsia is typical of the neovascular form
In the atrophic form, intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are given
In the neovascular form, intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are given

questions.note: AMD affects central vision (central scotoma, difficulty reading/recognising faces); peripheral vision is preserved. Wet (neovascular) AMD: sudden metamorphopsia → intravitreal anti-VEGF. Dry (atrophic) AMD: no anti-VEGF (AREDS vitamins, low-vision aids). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Complications of retinal vein occlusion are:
questions.note: RVO: macular oedema (the main cause of visual loss – anti-VEGF), retinal/iris neovascularisation → vitreous haemorrhage and neovascular glaucoma (ischaemic forms → PRP). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In central retinal artery occlusion:

o.t: The direct pupillary light reflex is normal
The direct pupillary light reflex disappears

questions.note: CRAO: pale ischaemic retina with cherry-red spot, near-total loss of vision → afferent defect (direct reflex abolished/RAPD, consensual preserved). Painless. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Retinal detachment can be produced by:
questions.note: Rhegmatogenous RD → retinal break; tractional RD → proliferative DR (fibrovascular membranes); exudative RD → tumours, inflammation. (Cataract SURGERY is a risk factor, not cataract itself.) (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are indicated in:
questions.note: Anti-VEGF (ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab, faricimab): wet AMD, diabetic macular oedema, macular oedema of RVO, myopic CNV; also used as adjunct in proliferative DR and neovascular glaucoma. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the ocular complications of a branch retinal vein thrombosis:
questions.note: BRVO: macular oedema (main cause of VA loss) and retinal neovascularisation → vitreous haemorrhage. Neovascular glaucoma is mainly a complication of ischaemic CRVO, rare in BRVO. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In retinitis pigmentosa:

o.t: The visual field is concentrically constricted
The visual field shows a central scotoma
The patient does not see well at night

questions.note: RP: night blindness (rods first), ring scotoma → concentric ("tunnel") constriction, bone-spicule pigment, attenuated vessels, waxy pale disc; ERG extinguished. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In age-related macular degeneration one may have:
questions.note: AMD affects the macula → central scotoma, metamorphopsia, difficulty reading; it is the leading cause of legal blindness in the elderly (not rare). Peripheral vision is preserved. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the onset of vision loss in ischemic optic neuropathy?
questions.note: Ischaemic optic neuropathy: sudden, painless loss of vision (often noticed on waking), with altitudinal field defect and swollen disc.

questions.q: Which of the following systemic treatments may be used for ischemic optic neuropathy?
questions.note: Non-arteritic AION has no proven treatment; control of vascular risk factors and antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) are used. Arteritic AION = high-dose corticosteroids.

questions.q: Optic nerve atrophy may result from:
questions.note: Consecutive/secondary optic atrophy: glaucoma (cupped atrophy), after optic neuritis/papillitis or uveitis involving the disc, extensive retinal damage (retinal detachment, RP, CRAO). Cataract and conjunctivitis do not damage the nerve.

questions.q: In a retrobulbar neuritis the fundus presents:
questions.note: Retrobulbar neuritis: "the patient sees nothing and the doctor sees nothing" – the fundus (disc) is normal at onset.

questions.q: In the anterior inflammatory optic neuropathy the fundus reveals:
questions.note: Anterior inflammatory optic neuropathy (papillitis): hyperaemic (congested), swollen disc with blurred margins. Pallor appears later (atrophy).

questions.q: Retrobulbar optical uveitis is characterised by:

o.t: central scotoma of the visual field

questions.note: Retrobulbar optic neuritis: decreased VA, central scotoma, dyschromatopsia, pain on eye movement, NORMAL disc at onset.

questions.q: causes of consecutive optical artrophy
questions.note: Consecutive (secondary) optic atrophy follows disease of the retina/choroid (RP, extensive chorioretinitis) or of the disc itself (papillitis, AION).

questions.q: Causes of secondary optic nerve atrophy:
questions.note: Optic atrophy: trauma, glaucoma (cupped atrophy), compression (pituitary adenoma → descending/primary atrophy), optic neuritis, ischaemia, chorioretinal diseases (consecutive). Anterior uveitis does not.

questions.q: Causes of bilateral papilloedema include:
questions.note: Bilateral papilloedema = raised intracranial pressure: tumours, hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis), subarachnoid haemorrhage, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, venous sinus thrombosis. CRVO and orbital cellulitis are unilateral.

questions.q: In edematous neuropathy the visual acuity is

o.t: Normal for a long period of time

questions.note: Papilloedema (oedematous disc from raised ICP): VA stays NORMAL for a long time (only transient obscurations), unlike papillitis/AION.

questions.q: The causes of optic nerve atrophy are:
questions.note: Optic atrophy: glaucoma, ischaemic and inflammatory optic neuropathies, compression, trauma, toxic. Cataract and iridocyclitis do not cause it.

questions.q: Manifestations of retrobulbar optic neuropathy can be
questions.note: Retrobulbar optic neuritis: decreased VA, central scotoma, dyschromatopsia (red desaturation), RAPD, pain on eye movement; field is abnormal; hemianopia = chiasm/retrochiasmal.

questions.q: The optic disc:

o.t: Is located at the centre of the retina

questions.note: The optic disc lies ≈ 3 mm nasal to the fovea; it contains the axons of ganglion cells (not their cell bodies) and no photoreceptors (blind spot); normally pink with sharp margins. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the visual field change typical of retrobulbar (inflammatory) optic neuritis:
questions.note: Optic neuritis (often MS): sudden VA loss, pain on eye movement, RAPD, red desaturation, CENTRAL or centro-caecal scotoma, normal disc in the retrobulbar form. Altitudinal defects = AION; enlarged blind spot = papilloedema. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In absolute pupillary rigidity:

o.t: The lesion is on the afferent pathway of the pupillary reflex
The lesion is on the efferent pathway of the pupillary reflex
The direct pupillary reflex is normal
The direct pupillary reflex is abolished

questions.note: Absolute rigidity = efferent (III / parasympathetic) lesion: the pupil reacts neither to direct, nor to consensual light, nor to near; vision is normal. Amaurotic rigidity = afferent lesion (blind eye), consensual preserved. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In anterior (ischaemic) optic neuropathy:

o.t: The optic disc has blurred margins
The optic disc shows an enlarged cup

questions.note: AION: sudden painless loss of vision, swollen (often sectoral) pale disc with blurred margins and splinter haemorrhages, altitudinal (usually inferior) field defect, RAPD. Later optic atrophy WITHOUT cupping (cupping = glaucoma). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The typical visual field change in anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is:
questions.note: AION damages the superior or inferior half of the disc (short posterior ciliary arteries) → altitudinal field defect, usually inferior. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Which eye diseases may appear as complications of Horton's disease (giant cell arteritis)?
questions.note: Giant cell arteritis: arteritic AION (most common, severe, may become bilateral), CRAO, cilioretinal artery occlusion, diplopia. Emergency: ESR/CRP, IV corticosteroids before temporal artery biopsy. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The typical visual field change in AION is:
questions.note: AION → altitudinal (usually inferior) defect. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In amaurotic pupillary rigidity:

o.t: The lesion is on the afferent pathway of the pupillary reflex
The lesion is on the efferent pathway of the pupillary reflex
The direct pupillary reflex is normal
The direct pupillary reflex is abolished

questions.note: Amaurotic rigidity = blind eye (retina/optic nerve lesion): no direct reflex, but consensual reflex preserved when the healthy eye is lit; the near reflex is preserved. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In optic atrophy:

o.t: There is an afferent pupillary defect
There is an efferent pupillary defect

questions.note: Optic atrophy: pale (white) disc, decreased VA, field defects and a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Posterior segment damage due to blunt ocular trauma may lead to:
questions.note: Blunt trauma, posterior segment: commotio retinae (Berlin oedema), retinal haemorrhages, retinal tears/dialysis → detachment, choroidal rupture/haemorrhage, vitreous haemorrhage, optic nerve avulsion. Iridodialysis is anterior segment; pterygium is degenerative.

questions.q: Hyphema is:

o.t: a horizontal level of blood within the anterior chamber
a horizontal level of inflammatory cells within the anterior chamber

questions.note: Hyphaema = blood in the anterior chamber with a horizontal level (hypopyon = pus/inflammatory cells).

questions.q: Iridodialisis represents:

o.t: Medial ruptures of the pupillary margins
The detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body

questions.note: Iridodialysis = disinsertion of the iris root from the ciliary body (D-shaped pupil, possible monocular diplopia).

questions.q: Iridodialysis represents:

o.t: medial ruptures of the pupillary margin
the detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body

questions.note: Iridodialysis = detachment of the iris root from the ciliary body.

questions.q: Ocular burns:

o.t: acid burns produce liquefaction of the tissue albumin
local irrigation with water is mandatory
local irrigation with water is not indicated

questions.note: Ocular burns: physical (thermal, UV, radiation) or chemical; immediate copious irrigation with water/saline is mandatory. ACIDS coagulate proteins (barrier); ALKALIS cause liquefaction (more severe, penetrate).

questions.q: The acid burns produces:
questions.note: Acids → coagulation necrosis (precipitated proteins limit penetration); alkalis → liquefactive necrosis (saponification, deep penetration).

questions.q: Sympathetic ophtalmia is caused by:
questions.note: Sympathetic ophthalmia = bilateral granulomatous panuveitis after penetrating injury (or surgery) of one eye, involving uveal tissue.

questions.q: Sympathetic ophthalmia is caused by
questions.note: Sympathetic ophthalmia follows penetrating injury (or intraocular surgery) of the exciting eye.

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Contusion of the eye with a bullet can produce:
questions.note: Ocular contusion: traumatic mydriasis, lens subluxation/dislocation, commotio retinae (retinal oedema), contusion cataract, hyphaema, choroidal rupture. Neovascular glaucoma is ischaemic, not traumatic.

questions.q: Chemical burns of the eyes – choose the true statements:

o.t: Punctate erosions are the only corneal lesions
The first therapeutic gesture is neutralization with complementary substances
They are frequently cured with corneal leucoma
Eyes should be flushed immediately with plenty of water

questions.note: Severe chemical burns: limbal necrosis/ischaemia (prognostic), extensive epithelial loss, often heal with corneal leucoma/vascularisation; first gesture = immediate copious irrigation with water (no attempts at neutralisation).

also: Old exam (English version of the French paper)
questions.q: Attitude in treating traumatic ocular perforation has to be:

o.t: Ocular massage for draining the pus
Radiology for finding an intraocular foreign body

questions.note: Open-globe injury: endophthalmitis prophylaxis, imaging for IOFB, watertight primary suture as soon as possible; never massage/press the eye; do not delay surgery.

questions.q: Burning sensation after bicycling, fluorescein shows vertical corneal erosions. Diagnosis:
questions.note: Vertical linear corneal erosions (scratches) = foreign body under the upper eyelid → evert the lid and remove it.

questions.q: In eye chemical burns the following are observed:

o.t: Limbal necrosis indicates the severity of the burn
Neutralization of the chemical is necessary
Abundant local irrigation is indicated only at the hospital, to avoid supra-infection

questions.note: Chemical burns: limbal ischaemia/necrosis = severity marker; corneal erosions; irrigate IMMEDIATELY on the spot with plenty of water (not neutralisation, not waiting for hospital); VA is frequently decreased.

questions.q: A young man is hit in his eye with a tennis ball. Possible eye injuries include all with one exception:

o.t: Endophthalmitis in case of scleral rupture

questions.note: Tennis-ball contusion: iridodialysis, commotio retinae (Berlin oedema), vitreous haemorrhage, globe rupture (with endophthalmitis risk); meibomitis is not traumatic.

questions.q: A 20-year-old patient has decreased vision after blunt trauma. Causes of the visual loss can be:
questions.note: Contusion can cause hyphaema, lens subluxation/luxation, commotio retinae, retinal tears/detachment, choroidal rupture, optic nerve avulsion. Subconjunctival haemorrhage does not reduce vision; POAG is not post-traumatic (angle recession gives a secondary glaucoma years later). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In third-degree chemical eye burns, one may observe:
questions.note: Severe (grade III–IV) burns: limbal ischaemia/necrosis, blanched white conjunctiva (ischaemia, not congestion), large epithelial defect, opaque cornea, poor VA; frequent sequelae (symblepharon, vascularised leucoma, dry eye). Staining is strongly positive. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The management of a penetrating eye injury should include:

o.t: Imaging (X-ray / CT) to find an intraocular foreign body

questions.note: Open globe: no pressure on the eye (no massage), rigid shield, systemic/intravitreal antibiotics (endophthalmitis prophylaxis), tetanus prophylaxis, CT/X-ray for an IOFB, urgent primary watertight repair – surgery is NOT delayed. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: A 20-year-old patient has decreased vision after blunt trauma. Causes of the visual loss can be:
questions.note: Blunt trauma: hyphaema, traumatic mydriasis, lens subluxation, commotio retinae, retinal detachment, choroidal rupture, optic nerve avulsion/traumatic optic neuropathy. Amblyopia is developmental; angle-recession glaucoma appears years later. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: In third-degree chemical eye burns, one may observe:
questions.note: Severe burns: limbal ischaemia/necrosis, corneal erosions/epithelial loss, decreased VA, white ischaemic conjunctiva (marked congestion is a sign of mild burns), frequent sequelae (symblepharon, leucoma, neovascularisation). (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: Choose the possible complications of hyphaema:
questions.note: Hyphaema complications: rebleeding (days 3–5), raised IOP / secondary glaucoma (blocked trabeculum), corneal blood staining (haematocornea – the most severe), optic atrophy from prolonged high IOP. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: An iron intraocular foreign body must be removed:
questions.note: Iron (and copper) IOFBs are toxic: iron → siderosis bulbi (iris heterochromia, cataract, retinopathy, glaucoma). A metallic IOFB must always be removed, as early as possible, before complications develop. (Translated from the French section.)

questions.q: The most serious complication of hyphaema is:
questions.note: Corneal blood staining (favoured by a total hyphaema + high IOP) can permanently opacify the cornea and causes amblyopia in children. (Some sources consider secondary glaucoma; the classic answer of this exam is haematocornea.) (Translated from the French section.)

cards.q: What does a pinhole test tell you?
cards.a: VA improves with pinhole → refractive error; no improvement → organic disease (cataract, macula, optic nerve).

cards.q: Visual field defect of a pituitary adenoma?
cards.a: Bitemporal (heteronymous) hemianopia – chiasmal compression of crossing nasal fibres.

cards.q: A left homonymous hemianopia localises where?
cards.a: Right retrochiasmal pathway (right optic tract, radiations or occipital cortex).
Congenital: X-linked, males, bilateral, symmetrical, stable, untreatable. Acquired: asymmetric, progressive, may improve.
Rods: periphery, night vision, rhodopsin. Cones: macula, day & colour vision, VA, iodopsin.

cards.q: Correction of myopia / hyperopia / astigmatism / presbyopia?
cards.a: Myopia: divergent (minus). Hyperopia: convergent (plus). Astigmatism: cylindrical/toric. Presbyopia: plus for near.
Retinal detachment, myopic maculopathy/CNV, glaucoma, early cataract, vitreous degeneration.

cards.q: When does presbyopia start, and in whom earlier?
cards.a: ~40–45 years; earlier in hyperopes, later in myopes.
1 Simultaneous perception, 2 fusion, 3 stereopsis.
Paralytic: acquired, diplopia, angle larger toward the paralysed muscle, limited movement. Concomitant: child, same angle, no diplopia, amblyopia.
Ptosis, eye down & out, mydriasis (pupil-involving → aneurysm until proven otherwise).
Remove cause + correct refraction + occlusion/atropine of the GOOD eye, before 7–8 y and before strabismus surgery.

cards.q: Orbital vs preseptal cellulitis – key sign?
cards.a: Proptosis (+ painful limited motility, chemosis, ± decreased VA/RAPD) = orbital cellulitis.

cards.q: Most common sign of thyroid eye disease?
cards.a: Upper eyelid retraction (Dalrymple); also lid lag, proptosis, restrictive diplopia.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for congenital dacryocystitis?
cards.a: Probing of the nasolacrimal duct (after massage + antibiotics).
Acute dacryoadenitis (inflamed lacrimal gland in the upper-outer lid).
Chalazion: chronic painless meibomian lipogranuloma. Hordeolum: acute painful staphylococcal abscess (external = Zeis).
Entropion: margin in → trichiasis, corneal erosions. Ectropion: margin out → epiphora, exposure (paralytic = VII).
Basal cell carcinoma (lower lid, medial canthus).

cards.q: Viral vs bacterial vs allergic conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Viral: watery, follicles, pre-auricular node. Bacterial: mucopurulent, papillae. Allergic: ITCHING, chemosis, papillae (giant = cobblestones).

cards.q: Onset of neonatal conjunctivitis by cause?
cards.a: Chemical day 1; gonococcal day 2–4; chlamydial day 5–14 → systemic antibiotics.

cards.q: Should you patch an eye with conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Never.

cards.q: HSV epithelial keratitis – sign and forbidden drug?
cards.a: Dendritic fluorescein-positive ulcer with reduced sensation; NO topical steroids (aciclovir/ganciclovir instead).
Vesicles on the tip of the nose in herpes zoster ophthalmicus → high risk of ocular involvement.

cards.q: Keratitis after a plant/tree branch injury?
cards.a: Think bacterial AND fungal keratitis: scrape for culture, intensive antimicrobials.
Ciliary injection, miosis, KP, flare & cells, hypopyon, posterior synechiae.
Topical steroids + mydriatic-cycloplegics (never miotics).
White fluffy focus next to a pigmented scar, vitritis ("headlight in the fog").
Phacolytic glaucoma, phaco-anaphylactic uveitis, lens luxation.
Posterior capsule opacification after extracapsular surgery → Nd:YAG capsulotomy.
Iridodonesis/phacodonesis, unequal AC depth, vitreous in AC, monocular diplopia.
10–21 mmHg; Goldmann applanation tonometry.
Painless, enlarged cup, arcuate/nasal field defects, raised IOP, VA preserved until late.

cards.q: Acute angle closure – signs and definitive treatment?
cards.a: Painful red eye, haloes, nausea, corneal oedema, mid-dilated fixed pupil, shallow AC, IOP 50–80 → laser iridotomy in BOTH eyes.
Epiphora, photophobia, blepharospasm (+ buphthalmos, cloudy cornea).
Retinal ischaemia: proliferative diabetic retinopathy, ischaemic CRVO, ocular ischaemic syndrome.
CRAO: pale retina, cherry-red spot, thin arteries. CRVO: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, tortuous veins, disc oedema.
Microaneurysms.

cards.q: Type of RD in proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
cards.a: Tractional.
Wet (neovascular) AMD – intravitreal anti-VEGF. Dry: AREDS, low-vision aids.
Floaters, flashes, progressive curtain-like field loss, VA loss if macula off.
Leukocoria (then strabismus).
Night blindness, tunnel vision, bone-spicule pigment, thin vessels, waxy pale disc.

cards.q: Typical field defects: optic neuritis / AION / papilloedema?
cards.a: Central scotoma / altitudinal defect / enlarged blind spot.
ESR/CRP and immediate high-dose systemic corticosteroids (temporal artery biopsy) – protect the other eye.
Amaurotic (afferent, blind eye): no direct, consensual kept. Absolute (efferent, III): no direct, no consensual, vision normal.

cards.q: First step in a chemical burn?
cards.a: Immediate copious irrigation with water/saline on the spot (≥ 30 min), no neutralisation.
Acids → coagulation (superficial). Alkalis → liquefaction (deep, more severe).
Corneal blood staining (haematocornea); also rebleeding and glaucoma.

cards.q: Open globe – what not to do?
cards.a: No pressure, no massage, no drops, no tonometry; shield + CT + antibiotics + urgent repair. No MRI if metallic IOFB.
Foreign body under the upper eyelid – evert the lid.

cards.q: Red reflex – what does a white reflex mean?
cards.a: Leukocoria: retinoblastoma, congenital cataract, ROP, Coats, PFV.

cards.q: How do you do digital tonometry?
cards.a: Patient looks down; two index fingers palpate the globe through the upper lid alternately; soft / normal / hard. Not in open globe.
Epithelial defects (green under cobalt blue); Seidel test for wound leak.
